forecast.title: Poll-of-polls and seat forecast: 2026 New Zealand general election
how_to_read: The poll average is where the public polls, adjusted for each pollster's habitual lean, put each party today. Its interval shows only how noisy the polls are.
The forecast interval is wider: it adds how far New Zealand's final polls have missed the result at the last five elections and how much support can still move before 7 November.

Seats come from running the real MMP rules (5% or an electorate seat, Sainte-Laguë, overhang) on tens of thousands of simulated results. Expected seats are an average; the 80% range is where 8 in 10 simulations land.
A bloc's 'majority' probability is the share of simulations in which those parties alone hold more than half of all seats, including overhang seats.
Probabilities are rounded to the nearest 1% and seats to whole numbers deliberately: the inputs are not precise enough to justify more.
A 70% chance is not a certainty: it means the other outcome happens about 3 times in 10.

blocs.bloc: Labour + Green + Te Pāti Māori + TOP

majority_threshold.note: 61 of 120; one more for every two overhang seats (62 of 122-123)

most_likely_parliament.note: The single most frequent exact seat combination across 40,000 simulations; with seven parties even the modal combination occurs in well under 1% of them, so read it as one plausible parliament, not a prediction.

pollsters.commissioner: Anacta Consulting (corporate clients; has polled for Labour)
Talbot Mills Research (corporate-client poll; also Labour's pollster, formerly UMR)
Curia Market Research (National's pollster) - publicly released polls not sponsored by the Taxpayers' Union

forecast.house_effects_note: House effect = that pollster's average deviation from the pooled trend this term, after shrinkage, in percentage points; positive = the pollster runs high for that party. Constrained to average zero across the independent public pollsters (1 News–Verian, RNZ–Reid Research, Roy Morgan, Taxpayers' Union–Curia, The Post/Freshwater Strategy), so they describe relative leans, not absolute bias. Party-commissioned/corporate polls (internal=true) get half weight and do not anchor the average.
forecast.undecided_note: All NZ pollsters publish party shares with undecided voters (typically 5-15%) excluded, so polls already sum to ~100% of decided voters and the aggregate is used as published. 'Others' are implied as 100 minus the seven listed parties. The historical calibration measures the resulting error directly, so no separate undecided adjustment is applied.

calibration.method: Final-3-weeks pooled average (sqrt(n) weights, no house adjustment) vs official result, per party; error SD modelled as k*sqrt(p(100-p))/10 fitted by least squares on squared errors (so historical bias widens the spread rather than shifting the mean).
calibration.correlation_note: Pairwise correlation of final-poll errors across the five elections (pairs with at least four shared elections), shrunk by n/(n+3) because five observations cannot pin down a correlation; matrix forced positive-definite.
calibration.drift_note: Random-walk innovation variance per day, estimated from week-to-week changes in this term's own trend (half attributed to real movement). Multiplied by days to the election.

electorates.note: Only electorates that can change the seat allocation are simulated: Epsom (ACT's insurance seat) and the seven Māori seats (Te Pāti Māori's party vote is far below 5%, so every seat it wins is an overhang seat; an independent or Te Tai Tokerau Party winner also changes the arithmetic). General seats won by National, Labour or the Greens are assumed never to exceed those parties' list entitlement, so they do not affect totals.

epsom.assumption: David Seymour (ACT) won Epsom by 8,142 votes in 2023 over Paul Goldsmith (National), who is standing again; National has not formally stood aside but did not campaign hard for the seat in 2023. ACT is polling 9-11% so Epsom only matters if ACT fell below 5%. Set at 90% (no 2026 Epsom poll).

Hauraki-Waikato.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Tāmaki Makaurau.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=1211) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Te Tai Hauāuru.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Te Tai Tokerau.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=1211) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Te Tai Tonga.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

Waiariki.simulation: shares_used = 0.7 x decided-voter shares from the electorate polls above (n_eff=500) + 0.3 x the same party's 2023 candidate-vote share; each candidate drawn with SD = sqrt(sampling + 9^2) points; winner = highest draw.

maori_seats_context: 2023: Te Pāti Māori won 6 of 7 (Tāmaki Makaurau by 42 votes, Te Tai Tokerau by 517); Labour held Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
6 Sep 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election: Oriini Kaipara (TPM) 6,948 beat Peeni Henare (Labour) 3,429 (turnout low). Kaipara stands again; Labour's candidate is Kerrin Leoni.

Nov 2025: Tākuta Ferris (Te Tai Tonga) and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau) were expelled from TPM; Kapa-Kingi was reinstated by the High Court, then left in May 2026 to found Te Tai Tokerau Party. Ferris stands as an independent.
Prior for Te Tai Tokerau and Te Tai Tonga: half of the 2023 Te Pāti Māori candidate vote is credited to the sitting MP's new vehicle (Te Tai Tokerau Party / independent) and half to Te Pāti Māori.
Electorate polls in Māori seats have small samples (n≈500) and a history of large misses; the 9-point systematic error term and the 30% weight on the 2023 result reflect that.

historical_track_record.note: What this model would have said two weeks before each election since 2011 (polls as of that date, house effects estimated from that term, calibration from the other four elections) versus the official result; plus the final-3-weeks simple pooled average, and how the governing party moved from mid-term (18 months out) to polling day.

caveats: Polling error: at the last five elections NZ's final polls missed individual parties by up to 5 points (National 2020). The forecast intervals are built from those misses, but a miss bigger than any since 2011 is always possible.

Threshold effects: TOP and NZ First sit near the 5% line, and Te Pāti Māori's seats depend on a handful of Māori-electorate contests. A one-point shift can move 6-10 seats between blocs, which is why the bloc probabilities are far less certain than the vote shares.
Electorate assumptions: Epsom and the Māori seats are modelled from very few, small-sample electorate polls and stated assumptions; those probabilities are the model's weakest input.
Late swing: a fifth of voters typically decide in the final fortnight; advance voting (which opened 26 Oct) blunts but does not remove this.
Undecideds: polls exclude 5-15% undecided voters; if they break unevenly the published shares shift.
House effects are relative to the average public pollster, not to the truth; if all pollsters share a bias (as in 2020) the aggregate shares it.
Party-commissioned and corporate-client polls (Talbot Mills, Anacta, Curia) are published selectively and are down-weighted, but may still colour the average.
The model does not forecast coalition negotiations: a 'majority' means the seats exist, not that the parties would agree to govern together.
Only seven parties are modelled; a minor party winning an electorate or crossing 5% from nowhere is not simulated.

simulation.distribution: multivariate logit-normal around the poll average

parties.name: New Zealand National Party
parties.tagline: In government 2023–26. Proposes no new taxes next term and a surplus by 2028/29, compulsory KiwiSaver from birth, and splitting Foodstuffs into two companies.
parties.in_a_nutshell: National leads the government now, with ACT and NZ First. It wants to keep taxes where they are, cut government debt and get the books back in surplus. It is promising compulsory KiwiSaver, longer paid parental leave and changes to sentencing and consent law.

big_ideas.text: No new taxes next term, and the government's books back in surplus by 2028/29
Make KiwiSaver compulsory for workers and sign babies up at birth
Split Foodstuffs (New World, Pak'nSave, Four Square) into two separate companies to boost supermarket competition
Extend paid parental leave from 26 to 30 weeks
An extra $604 million for medicines (Pharmac) and free bowel screening from age 50, paid for partly by cutting foreign aid outside the Pacific
Replace NCEA, make students finish Year 11, and limit screen time for young children at school

Sentencing and consent law: no 'good character' sentence discounts for sexual offending, an active 'yes' required for consent, and a penalty for refusing to give information when a child has been killed

they_say.text: National's slogan is "Fixing the Basics, Building the Future"; its fiscal plan says a re-elected National government will "not impose new taxes" and will "return to surplus in 2028/29 and stay there".
they_say.attribution: National Party (fiscal plan, 12 Oct 2026; slogan as reported by policy.nz)

critics_say.text: Labour says "National promised to grow the economy and get the Government's finances in order. It has done neither - unemployment is higher, growth is weaker, debt has continued to rise, and frontline services have been cut."

current_seats.note: National won 49 seats in 2023 (48 at the general election plus the Port Waikato by-election). Papakura has been vacant since Judith Collins resigned on 14 May 2026 (no by-election is required within six months of a general election), so at dissolution National held 48 of the 122 sitting members in a 123-seat House (data/parliaments/54.json).

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Led the government since November 2023 (with ACT and NZ First) and from 2008 to 2017.
parties.track_record_line: Led the government since November 2023 (with ACT and NZ First) and from 2008 to 2017. Of 71 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 35 kept, 11 partly kept, 5 broken, 10 abandoned, 10 still in progress. (11 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to continue the current government with ACT and NZ First. Luxon ruled out a 'grand coalition' with Labour (May 2026) and formally ruled out any deal with Opportunity, including confidence and supply, from 27 July 2026, citing its plans to raise taxes; he repeated this through October.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (12 Oct 2026) keeps new spending to $2.4b a year, leaves $7.5b of operating money unallocated over four years, and part-funds promises by cutting foreign aid. It includes $1.2m for an election policy costings unit.

parties.name: New Zealand Labour Party
parties.tagline: In opposition 2023–26. Proposes up to three free GP visits a year funded by a capital gains tax on property, free prescriptions, and restoring the old pay-equity law.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Labour is the biggest opposition party and last governed from 2017 to 2023. It wants three free GP visits a year, paid for by a new tax on profits from selling property (not the family home). It also promises to restore pay equity and to give the Commerce Commission new powers over large companies' prices.

big_ideas.text: Up to three free GP visits a year, paid for by a 28% capital gains tax on property sales (family homes and farms excluded)
Free prescriptions, free cervical screening for ages 25-69 and free referred maternity scans
Restore the old pay-equity law and give 65,000 care and support workers a $4 an hour pay rise
Make price gouging illegal and require Woolworths and Foodstuffs to run their wholesale and retail businesses separately
Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in the three biggest cities ($10 elsewhere) and freeze fuel tax for three years
A 'NZ Future Fund' to invest in New Zealand businesses and infrastructure
Wipe 10% off eligible graduates' student loans and build at least 6,000 more social homes

they_say.text: Labour's slogan is "Better Starts Now". It says "every promise Labour has made is fully paid for" and that it "will balance the books without shrinking the economy".

critics_say.text: National's Nicola Willis called Labour's fiscal plan fraudulent, saying Treasury estimates restoring the old pay-equity scheme would cost $11 billion, leaving Labour about $8.5 billion short; Labour says it has enough unallocated money and won't name a figure during negotiations.
critics_say.attribution: Nicola Willis, National finance spokesperson (via RNZ)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Led governments from 1999 to 2008 and 2017 to 2023; in opposition since 2023.
parties.track_record_line: Led governments from 1999 to 2008 and 2017 to 2023; in opposition since 2023. Of 71 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 36 kept, 10 partly kept, 7 broken, 18 abandoned. (21 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Will keep working with the Greens and says its 'door is open' to Opportunity. It has ruled out NZ First (formally, 10 Aug 2026) and ACT. It says it could work with Te Pāti Māori but senior roles for them are 'unlikely', and Hipkins ruled out giving the Greens or Te Pāti Māori the police or corrections portfolios (14 Oct 2026). Its campaign chair says his preference is a government with just the Greens and Opportunity.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (Oct 2026), reviewed by accounting firm Hall Chadwick, keeps the $2.4b operating allowance, forecasts a surplus in 2028/29 and aims for net debt below 20% of GDP. National disputes how pay equity, fuel tax and the Future Fund are accounted for.

parties.notes: Campaign development, 23 Oct 2026: Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate Kerrin Leoni resigned as a candidate after Te Ao Māori News published footage of her campaigning at a gathering attended by Mongrel Mob members. Hipkins said the footage was "inconsistent with the standards I expect of Labour candidates". Her name stays on the ballot because nominations had closed (1News, 23 Oct 2026). Candidate-level events for other parties are recorded in electorates/ and people profiles, not on these cards.

parties.name: Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand
parties.tagline: In opposition 2023–26. Proposes a wealth tax above $10 million to fund income tax cuts, a 2% yearly cap on rent rises, and a government-owned supermarket chain.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Greens want strong action on climate change and nature, and more help for people on low incomes. They would tax people with more than $10 million in wealth and cut income tax for most workers. They also want a government-owned supermarket and limits on rent rises.

big_ideas.text: A 2.5% yearly tax on wealth above $10 million and a tax on large inheritances and gifts, so most workers can get an income tax cut (first $10,000 tax-free)
Cap rent rises at 2% a year and build many more public homes
'KiwiMart': require Foodstuffs and Woolworths to sell at least 120 stores to a new government-owned supermarket chain
Free public transport for children, students, apprentices and Community Services Card holders, and $2 fares for everyone else
A new publicly owned company, 'Kiwipower', to build renewable energy
An extra $3 billion a year for health, and restore pay equity for care workers
Keep and expand free school lunches and make early childhood education free

they_say.text: The Greens' slogan is "For All of Us". Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says the government's current budget path is "made possible only through underinvestment in core public services".
they_say.attribution: Green Party; Chlöe Swarbrick (fiscal plan launch, 23 Oct 2026)

critics_say.text: National's campaign chair Simeon Brown says the Greens' plan contains "nine new taxes"; the Greens' own fiscal plan shows net core Crown debt about $26.6 billion higher than Treasury's forecast by 2030/31.
critics_say.attribution: Simeon Brown, National (via B2B News); Green fiscal plan figures

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Never a full coalition partner; supported Labour-led governments in 2017-2020 (confidence and supply, with ministers outside Cabinet) and 2020-2023 (cooperation agreement).
parties.track_record_line: Never a full coalition partner; supported Labour-led governments in 2017-2020 (confidence and supply, with ministers outside Cabinet) and 2020-2023 (cooperation agreement). Of 22 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 11 kept, 4 partly kept, 6 broken, 1 abandoned. (10 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Campaigning to change the government with Labour: the two parties held a joint stand-up at Waitangi in February 2026 to show they would work together. Co-leader Marama Davidson said the Greens had stayed in contact with Te Pāti Māori through its internal troubles. We found no formal Green statement this campaign ruling other parties in or out.
coalition_stance_2026.note: We found no explicit Green statement on working with Opportunity, National, ACT or NZ First.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (23 Oct 2026), with direct fiscal effects reviewed by Infometrics, raises about $28.75b over four years from new taxes, lifts yearly new spending to $4.5-4.7b, delays surplus to 2029/30, and has net core Crown debt reaching $256.4b (44% of GDP) by 2030/31.

parties.name: ACT New Zealand
parties.tagline: In government 2023–26. Proposes merging 43 government departments into 19, raising the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, and repealing the Zero Carbon Act.
parties.in_a_nutshell: ACT is part of the current government with National and NZ First. It wants the government to spend less, have fewer ministries and deliver public services by need rather than ethnicity (its phrase is 'one law for all'). It would slowly raise the pension age to 67 and scrap the net-zero climate law.

big_ideas.text: A smaller government: merge 43 departments into 19 and abolish ministries for particular groups (such as women, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities)
Raise the pension (NZ Super) age gradually to 67 by 2035
Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and the net-zero target, and abolish the Climate Change Commission
Freeze the minimum wage for three years and bring in a lower training wage
Three strikes for burglary and deporting serious offenders who aren't citizens
Let pharmacists treat more illnesses and lift Pharmac's share of the health budget
Remove ethnicity-based criteria from public services and close the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are settled

they_say.text: ACT says "New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand's potential."
they_say.attribution: ACT New Zealand ('A Smaller, More Affordable Government')

critics_say.text: The Greens called ACT's fiscal plan "welfare for the wealthiest" and Labour accused ACT of "punching down", after it proposed raising the pension age and spending $653 million less on disability benefits.
critics_say.attribution: Green Party and Labour Party (via RNZ)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: In coalition government with National and NZ First since 2023; supported National-led governments 2008-2017.
parties.track_record_line: In coalition government with National and NZ First since 2023; supported National-led governments 2008-2017. Of 33 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 18 kept, 4 partly kept, 5 broken, 6 abandoned. (5 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to keep the current government and 'lock Labour out'. Seymour said a four-party deal including Opportunity, if it crossed 5%, 'would be a good outcome' to keep the Greens and Te Pāti Māori out of power (16 Oct 2026). Labour has ruled ACT out.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (11 Oct 2026) promises lower debt and spending, including raising the pension age by three months a year and $653m less on disability benefits. RNZ noted two items (about $100m a year, and tax relief of $264m-$303m a year) were not explained.

parties.name: New Zealand First

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia's opening sentence calls it a "right-wing populist" party; the infobox lists right-wing populism, nationalism and social conservatism as its ideology.
position.note: Wikipedia editors have not agreed a position label

parties.tagline: In government 2023–26. Proposes splitting the big power companies' generation and retail arms, splitting Foodstuffs into two cooperatives, and buying back the BNZ.
parties.in_a_nutshell: NZ First is part of the current government and has been in government with both Labour and National in the past. It wants some benefits, like the pension and voting, kept for citizens only. It also wants to break up the big power companies and buy back the BNZ bank.

big_ideas.text: Split the big power companies' generation and retail businesses
Split Foodstuffs into two cooperatives and give the Commerce Commission more power
Buy back the Bank of New Zealand (BNZ) into public ownership
Only citizens could vote and get NZ Super; citizens first for social housing
A $5,000-a-year 'Kiwi Kids Grant' for a child's first three years, and $70 a week more Working for Families tax credit
Cut company tax to 20% for small and medium businesses
A binding referendum on the Māori seats and replacing the Waitangi Tribunal with a completion commission

they_say.text: Winston Peters says "what is needed more than anything else is serious skill, and serious experience in the next government" and that "It is vital that the left does not win."

critics_say.text: The NZ Herald reports NZ First is the largest party in Parliament not publishing a fiscal plan; a Green Party analysis put its policies at about $71.6 billion over four years, which NZ First rejects without giving its own figures. Labour's Chris Hipkins accused the party of "overt racism" when ruling it out.
critics_say.attribution: NZ Herald (22 Oct 2026); Green Party analysis; Chris Hipkins, Labour (10 Aug 2026)

parties.track_record_context: In government four times: with National (1996-98, 2023-26) and with Labour (confidence and supply 2005-08, coalition 2017-20).
parties.track_record_line: In government four times: with National (1996-98, 2023-26) and with Labour (confidence and supply 2005-08, coalition 2017-20). Of 43 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 21 kept, 3 partly kept, 7 broken, 9 abandoned, 3 still in progress. (7 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Has repeatedly ruled out Labour and is campaigning to continue the current National-led government. After the NZ Herald 'power brokers' debate (21 Oct 2026) Peters said 'No, I can't' when asked if he could sit at a Cabinet table with Opportunity's Qiulae Wong. Labour has also ruled NZ First out (10 Aug 2026).

costings.summary: No full fiscal plan. The NZ Herald (22 Oct 2026) says NZ First is the largest party in Parliament not publishing one. It has costed some items itself, e.g. about $1b a year for the small-business tax cut and $7.5b to buy back the BNZ (the Herald reports other estimates as high as $24b, without naming their source).

parties.name: Te Pāti Māori
parties.tagline: In opposition 2023–26. Proposes making the first $30,000 of income tax-free with a wealth tax, taking GST off food, and an independent Te Tiriti Commission.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Te Pāti Māori wants Māori to have more say over their own lives and resources, based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Its plan is to win the Māori electorate seats and to get people to give their party vote to Labour or the Greens. It would make the first $30,000 of income tax-free and add a wealth tax.

big_ideas.text: 'Kiwi Tax Plan': first $30,000 of income tax-free, a wealth tax, and a higher company tax rate
Take GST off food (kai)
An independent Te Tiriti Commission and binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations
Work towards a new constitution based on Matike Mai, and put the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into practice
Abolish prisons by 2040, replacing them with community-led solutions
A $1 billion fund for Māori and community ownership of renewable energy
A Māori Education Authority to run Māori education

they_say.text: Co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "There's one plan, two votes" and "The only way we're going to get this government out, get more Māori in Parliament, and continue to be the loudest, unapologetic, independent Māori voice is to focus on giving our votes to Te Pāti Māori candidates."
they_say.attribution: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (campaign launch, 16 Aug 2026, via RNZ)

critics_say.text: Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said Te Pāti Māori needs to "prove themselves to the country that they are worthy of being part of a government", after a year in which the party split and expelled two MPs.

current_seats.note: Won 6 electorates in 2023; MPs Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris were expelled in Nov 2025 (Kapa-Kingi now leads the Te Tai Tokerau Party; Ferris sits as an independent).

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Supported National-led governments under confidence-and-supply deals from 2008 to 2017 (as the Māori Party); in opposition since 2020.
parties.track_record_line: Supported National-led governments under confidence-and-supply deals from 2008 to 2017 (as the Māori Party); in opposition since 2020. Of 15 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 8 kept, 3 partly kept, 3 broken, 1 abandoned. (6 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to remove the current government and asks supporters to give their party vote to the 'left bloc' (Labour or the Greens). Responding to Labour saying senior roles were 'unlikely', co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said "Te Pāti Māori will have that conversation on 8th November."

issues.title: Cost of living
issues.why_it_matters: Prices for things like petrol, power and food have been rising faster than the Reserve Bank's 1-3% target. It is the number one worry for voters this year. Parties disagree on whether the answer is more competition, tax changes or direct help with bills.

key_facts.fact: Prices rose 3.7% in the year to the September 2026 quarter (down from 4.1% in June), above the Reserve Bank's 1-3% target.
Petrol was the biggest driver, up 19.1% on a year earlier in the CPI; electricity was up 9.3% and council rates 6.2%.
Food prices rose 2.4% in the year to September 2026.
61% of people named cost of living as a top issue facing the country, more than any other issue (Ipsos, May 2026). It was still number one in September.

Two companies, Foodstuffs and Woolworths, have about 82% of the grocery market (2025 figure); the Commerce Commission's 2022 market study described the sector as a duopoly in which competition was 'not working well for consumers'.

national.summary: Split Foodstuffs into two competing companies, hold fuel tax and road user charges until 2028, and keep council rate rises between 2% and 4% a year.

labour.summary: Make price gouging illegal, require the big supermarkets to separate wholesale from retail, cap public transport at $20 a week in the big cities, freeze fuel tax, and regulate hidden fees and hard-to-cancel subscriptions.

green.summary: Create a government-owned supermarket chain ('KiwiMart') from 120 stores the big two must sell, $2 public transport fares, and make the first $10,000 of income tax-free.

act.summary: Opposes breaking up the supermarkets; instead wants a one-stop consenting body so new competitors can open, and to accept overseas food labels by default.

nz-first.summary: Split Foodstuffs into two cooperatives, give the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner more power, and raise the Working for Families in-work tax credit by $70 a week.

te-pati-maori.summary: Take GST off food and back Māori-owned supermarkets and food sellers.

opportunity.summary: Give the Commerce Commission stronger powers against monopolies and duopolies, and pay most adults a regular Citizen's Income.

alliance.summary: Make the first $20,000 of income tax-free and bring electricity back into full public ownership to bring bills down.

conservative.summary: Lower GST to 12.5% and cut income and company taxes.

vision-nz.summary: Make the first $25,000 of income tax-free to give working families relief.

issues.title: Health
issues.why_it_matters: Health is voters' second-biggest worry. About a quarter of emergency department patients wait more than six hours, and hospital beds per person have fallen over the past decade. Parties offer different mixes of free visits, more staff, more medicines funding and new ways of delivering care.

key_facts.fact: 76.3% of emergency department patients were admitted, discharged or transferred within six hours in April-June 2026, up from 73.9% a year earlier; the government target is 95% by 2030.
72.6% of patients waited less than four months for planned (elective) treatment in April-June 2026, up from 63.9% a year earlier.
Hospital bed supply fell from 2.7 to 2.5 inpatient beds per 1,000 people between 2014 and 2024, and ED visits rose 21% over a decade (Australasian College for Emergency Medicine).
39% of people named healthcare as a top issue (Ipsos, May 2026), second only to cost of living.

national.summary: An extra $604 million for Pharmac medicines, free bowel screening from age 50 and breast screening to 74 by 2029, free cervical screening, and more training for rural doctors and nurses.

labour.summary: Up to three free GP visits a year (paid for by a capital gains tax), free prescriptions, free cervical screening and maternity scans, a job for every NZ-trained graduate nurse, and an emergency department recovery plan.

green.summary: An extra $3 billion a year for health, more free public health services, more Pharmac funding and free mental health services for all communities.

act.summary: Let pharmacists treat more conditions, lift Pharmac's share of the health budget above 10% by 2033, pay GPs more, and build two cancer centres through public-private partnership.

nz-first.summary: Give GPs more independence and less paperwork, make health coaches part of primary care, and review national nutrition guidelines.

te-pati-maori.summary: Invest in Māori health outcomes and whānau-led care for Māori children.

opportunity.summary: A 10-year plan for the health system made with health professionals, lifting health funding to 9% of GDP, and tougher rules on tobacco, vaping, alcohol and unhealthy food.

alliance.summary: Free GP, dental, optical and hearing care through a new public Community Health Service.

vision-nz.summary: Move health money from administration and 'race-based spending' to frontline services such as GPs and specialists.

te-tai-tokerau-party.summary: An independent, iwi-governed Māori health authority and a bonded scholarship scheme to train more Māori health workers.

conservative.summary: Make cutting hospital waiting times the top health priority, paid for with savings from bureaucracy and procurement.

womens-rights.summary: Ban puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s with 'sex-related distress' and restrict funded gender surgery to over-25s.

issues.title: Economy and jobs
issues.why_it_matters: Unemployment is at its highest level in about 11 years, and growth has been slow. The government's books are still in deficit. Parties split on whether to cut spending, change taxes or invest more to create jobs.

key_facts.fact: Unemployment was 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter (171,000 people), the highest since 2015.
The economy grew 0.2% in the June 2026 quarter and 1.7% over the year to June; GDP per person rose 0.1% over the year.
Treasury's pre-election update (PREFU, September 2026) forecasts the government's books returning to surplus in 2028/29, with net debt peaking at 43.9% of GDP in 2028.
Unemployment rose from fifth to fourth place in voters' list of top concerns (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: Keep spending tight to return to surplus, double export earnings by 2034 through new trade deals, keep the 'Investment Boost' tax break for business equipment, and cut compliance for small businesses.

labour.summary: A 'NZ Future Fund' to invest in New Zealand firms and infrastructure, a $4 billion building programme, faster payment of small-business invoices, more government contracts for local firms, and yearly minimum wage rises.

green.summary: Guarantee a job, training or study place for 16-24-year-olds out of work for six months, create jobs in nature restoration, and make union membership the default for new workers.

act.summary: Cut government spending, freeze the minimum wage for three years, add a lower training wage, and limit personal grievance claims.

nz-first.summary: Cut company tax to 20% for firms with turnover under $30 million, create a special economic zone at Marsden Point, and survey the whole country for minerals.

te-pati-maori.summary: Grow the Māori economy, including a $1 billion fund for Māori and community-owned renewable energy.

opportunity.summary: Lift science and innovation funding to 2% of GDP and strengthen competition law to help small businesses.

alliance.summary: Full employment, a 35-hour working week with no loss of pay, and a new 'KiwiWorks' Ministry of Works.

conservative.summary: Lower personal and company tax rates to encourage business investment.

womens-rights.summary: Pay equity in both the public and private sectors, and bring back Fair Pay Agreements.

issues.title: Housing and rent
issues.why_it_matters: Buying a first home is still out of reach for many people, and rents take a big share of income. House prices have eased a little but remain high. Parties differ on building more public housing, helping first-home buyers, and controlling rents.

key_facts.fact: The national median house price was $755,000 in September 2026, down 2.3% on a year earlier; Auckland's was $950,000.
The national median weekly rent on Trade Me was $625 in August 2026, the first year-on-year rise in 18 months.
Homes took a median of 46 days to sell in September 2026, three days longer than a year earlier.
Housing was the fifth-biggest concern for voters in September 2026 (Ipsos).

national.summary: Let more first-home buyers get 5% deposit loans, speed up building consents, change how developers pay for infrastructure, and make granny flats easier to build.

labour.summary: At least 6,000 more social homes over four years, a bigger Crown guarantee for community housing builders, and keeping rough sleepers out of the 'move on' law.

green.summary: Cap rent rises at 2% a year, a rental warrant of fitness, many more public homes, and reverse interest-deductibility tax breaks for landlords.

act.summary: Let residential landlords offset rental losses against their other income.

nz-first.summary: Put citizens first for social housing and require fast-tracked housing developments to include roads, water and other infrastructure.

te-pati-maori.summary: Build more public and private housing, and add a 5% stamp duty on residential sales and taxes on vacant houses and land banking.

opportunity.summary: Reform zoning to allow more homes and use a land value tax to make land banking unprofitable and lower house prices.

alliance.summary: A five-year public building programme led by Kāinga Ora to clear the social housing waitlist, with social rents capped at 25% of income.

nz-outdoors-freedom.summary: Free up land for subdivisions and revise resource-management rules to speed up house building, using a mix of public and private housing.

vision-nz.summary: Open government land for affordable housing and allow two homes to be built on a section under planning rules.

issues.title: Tax
issues.why_it_matters: Tax is one of the clearest dividing lines this election. Some parties promise no new taxes; others want new taxes on wealth, property or land to pay for services or income tax cuts. Concern about tax has been rising in polls.

key_facts.fact: New Zealand's top income tax rate is 39% on income over $180,000. There is no general capital gains tax (the 'bright-line' rule taxes gains on residential investment property sold within two years), and no wealth tax or inheritance tax.
45% of people say they pay about the right amount of tax and 44% want to pay less (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

In the same survey, 64% supported a 2.5% wealth tax on assets above $10 million (excluding family homes), 45% supported a capital gains tax on property (excluding the family home), and less than a quarter supported a land tax.

national.summary: No new taxes next term; delays any new tax cuts until debt is under control.

labour.summary: A 28% capital gains tax on residential and commercial property (not the family home) to fund GP visits; rules out raising GST in 2027.

green.summary: A 2.5% wealth tax on net assets above $10 million, a 33% tax on inheritances and gifts over $1 million, 33% company tax for the biggest firms, a new rate above $160,000, and the first $10,000 of income tax-free.

act.summary: No tax on KiwiSaver earnings, let landlords offset rental losses, and remove the cap on tax deductions for charitable donations.

nz-first.summary: Cut company tax from 28% to 20% for businesses with turnover under $30 million.

te-pati-maori.summary: Make the first $30,000 tax-free, add a 48% rate above $300,000, a wealth tax, a higher company tax rate and a 5% tax on profits sent overseas.

opportunity.summary: A 'Tax Reset': a land value tax (1.75% a year on urban land in the full plan, starting at 0.5% on urban land only and phased in over about a decade) funding a Citizen's Income, with income tax realigned to three rates.

alliance.summary: First $20,000 tax-free, a 2.5% wealth tax above $2 million, a 33% capital gains tax, a financial transactions levy and 30% company tax.

conservative.summary: Lower income and company taxes, GST at 12.5%, and no income tax on NZ Super.

vision-nz.summary: Make the first $25,000 tax-free and stop taxing superannuation and student loans.

issues.title: Power bills and fuel prices
issues.why_it_matters: A conflict in the Middle East pushed fuel prices up sharply this year, and electricity prices rose 9.3% in a year. Fuel prices jumped into voters' top four worries in May. Parties disagree on breaking up the big power companies, public ownership, and how much to rely on solar, oil and gas.

key_facts.fact: Petrol prices were 24.3% higher and diesel 55.8% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier, though below their April peak (Stats NZ).
Electricity prices rose 9.3% in the year to the September 2026 quarter.
Concern about fuel prices jumped 17 points to make it the fourth-biggest issue for voters (Ipsos, May 2026).

national.summary: Government-backed loans for home solar and batteries, let people sell their solar power to any buyer, require new data centres to bring their own power, and a back-up power contract for dry years.

labour.summary: Loans and subsidies for home solar (including for low and middle-income households), and closer scrutiny of fuel prices.

green.summary: A new publicly owned company, 'Kiwipower', to invest in renewable power, a clean-energy loan scheme, and legal plug-in solar with a renters' right to solar.

act.summary: Opposes breaking up the power companies; wants private investment in transmission, more domestic energy production, and households paid market rates for solar exports.

nz-first.summary: Split the big power companies' generation and retail arms, and offer fixed-price contracts for new power stations; invest in oil and gas exploration.

te-pati-maori.summary: A $1 billion fund for Māori and community-owned renewable energy, help for households to buy solar, and a national energy independence plan.

opportunity.summary: Restructure the electricity market to bring prices down and expand the grid to 30GW by 2050.

alliance.summary: Bring the whole electricity system - generation, lines and retail - into public ownership.

conservative.summary: Encourage cheap, abundant energy of all kinds, with no subsidies for any form of energy.

nz-loyal.summary: Energy independence, including oil and gas.

issues.title: Welfare and poverty
issues.why_it_matters: More children are living without basics like enough food or warm clothes than at any time since 2015. More people are on benefits as unemployment rises. Parties split between stricter obligations for people on benefits and higher or more universal payments.

key_facts.fact: 14.3% of children (about 169,300) lived in material hardship in the year to June 2025, the highest rate Stats NZ has recorded since 2015.
413,691 people were on a main benefit at the end of June 2026 (12.8% of working-age people), up 1.9% on a year earlier.
Poverty and inequality was named a top issue by 17% of people (Ipsos, May 2026).

national.summary: Drug testing for some beneficiaries, lower payments for people on a benefit for more than two years, a 26-week stand-down after leaving a job, and targeted work support for 30,000 jobseekers.

labour.summary: End annual benefit renewals for people with permanent disabilities, and repeal and replace the Disability Support Services Bill.

green.summary: Raise benefit payments, make the Best Start payment universal, strengthen Working for Families and expand ACC to cover income support.

act.summary: Tighten medical certificates for health-related benefits, monitor spending of long-term jobseekers, and stop new residents getting benefits for five years.

nz-first.summary: A $5,000-a-year Kiwi Kids Grant for each child's first three years (up to three children), $70 a week more Working for Families, and a 10-year benefit stand-down for new migrants.

te-pati-maori.summary: Make the first $30,000 of income tax-free and take GST off food to lift low incomes.

opportunity.summary: Replace most benefits with a Citizen's Income of up to $370 a week for most adults.

alliance.summary: A universal child benefit and a plan to eliminate child poverty by rebuilding universal social security.

te-tai-tokerau-party.summary: Wipe about $2 billion of debt low-income whānau owe to MSD and IRD and replace the benefit system with a simpler universal whānau allowance.

issues.title: Law and order
issues.why_it_matters: Crime and safety matter to many voters, and the current government has passed laws that lengthen sentences and restrict gangs. The prison population is growing. Parties range from longer sentences and more police to abolishing prisons and focusing on rehabilitation.

key_facts.fact: There were 11,240 people in prison in February 2026; the Ministry of Justice projects 15,200 by June 2036 if nothing changes, partly because of recent sentencing law changes.
Crime was named a top issue by 16% of people (Ipsos, May 2026); voters rated National the party most capable on crime (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: No 'good character' sentence discounts for sex offenders, a clear 'yes' required for consent, no right to silence when a child under 12 is killed, a police team for Auckland public transport, and more prison beds.

labour.summary: A new corporate manslaughter (corporate homicide) offence and an end to military-style 'boot camps' for young offenders.

green.summary: Focus on rehabilitation, end military-style academies, make coercive control a crime, and decriminalise cannabis for personal use.

act.summary: Add burglary to three-strikes sentencing, deport serious offenders who aren't citizens, expand rural policing and use noise cameras against boy racers.

nz-first.summary: Widen the grounds for deporting non-citizen criminals and ban public sales of fireworks.

te-pati-maori.summary: Abolish prisons by 2040, replacing them with community-led solutions and restorative justice.

opportunity.summary: More funding for courts and rehabilitation to cut reoffending, and decriminalise drug possession (but not supply).

conservative.summary: A Royal Commission of Inquiry into police performance and misconduct.

legalise-cannabis.summary: Stop prosecuting adults for cannabis and wipe past cannabis convictions.

te-tai-tokerau-party.summary: Move savings from empty prison beds into hapū-run rehabilitation sanctuaries with compulsory community work.

womens-rights.summary: Ban the 'rough sex' defence in murder cases, and replace the Prostitution Reform Act with the 'Nordic model' that criminalises buyers.

alliance.summary: 'Three strikes and into treatment': justice focused on rehabilitation, with no private prisons.

issues.title: Climate and environment
issues.why_it_matters: New Zealand has promised to cut greenhouse gases, and farming is the biggest source. The current government has eased some climate rules for farmers. Parties range from scrapping the net-zero target to putting farming into the emissions trading scheme.

key_facts.fact: Agriculture makes up about half of New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions.

In October 2025 the government set a new 2050 target to cut biogenic methane (mostly from farm animals) by 14-24% below 2017 levels, replacing the previous 24-47% range (enacted December 2025), and ruled out a tax on farm methane.
Voters rated the Greens as most capable on climate change and the environment (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: Keep farm emissions out of the emissions trading scheme, protect 50% of the ocean area New Zealand controls by 2040, and expand protection in the Hauraki Gulf.

labour.summary: Review the emissions trading scheme, keep backing the Paris Agreement, and work towards a Pacific agreement on climate.

green.summary: Cut gross emissions across all sectors including farming, phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, protect at least 30% of the ocean, and repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act.

act.summary: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and the net-zero goal, abolish the Climate Change Commission, keep farming out of emissions pricing, and count methane separately from carbon dioxide.

nz-first.summary: Expand mining and open conservation land to development, returning half of mining royalties to the regions.

te-pati-maori.summary: Ban seabed mining and invest in climate adaptation for the communities most at risk.

opportunity.summary: Put farming into a strengthened emissions trading scheme, keep the Climate Change Commission, ban seabed mining and build a $5 billion climate-resilience fund.

animal-justice.summary: Move away from animal farming with a farmer-led transition programme, citing livestock's share of emissions and water pollution.

conservative.summary: Leave the Paris Agreement and repeal climate-based laws and taxes.

nz-loyal.summary: End climate agreements, which it says are 'based on faulty science'.

nz-outdoors-freedom.summary: Withdraw from the Paris Agreement, focus on flood management and carbon-rich soils, and keep ecosystems free from poisons such as 1080.

alliance.summary: Replace the emissions trading scheme with a carbon tax, apply a strict 'polluter pays' rule, and ban mining on conservation land.

issues.title: Schools and education
issues.why_it_matters: The current government has changed the school curriculum and plans to replace NCEA. School attendance has improved but is still well below target. Parties argue about NCEA, school lunches, screens and student debt.

key_facts.fact: 64.3% of students attended school regularly in Term 2 2026, up from 58.4% a year earlier; the government's target is 80%.
Voters rated Labour as most capable on education (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: Replace NCEA with a new qualification, require students to finish Year 11, limit screens for young children, keep the cellphone ban, and extend school lunches to 2029.

labour.summary: Pause plans to scrap NCEA and set up an independent curriculum council, 1,000 more teacher aides, locally made school lunches, and 10% off eligible graduates' student loans.

green.summary: Keep and expand free school lunches, free early childhood education, reset the curriculum and NCEA changes, and fees-free tertiary study with universal student allowances.

act.summary: Expand charter schools, give teachers legal power to remove disruptive students, and create a pathway into the trades from school.

te-pati-maori.summary: A Māori Education Authority to run Māori education; it is also campaigning for compulsory te reo Māori in schools.

opportunity.summary: A 10-year education plan, more staff and support for early childhood education, and rebuilding the school lunch programme.

alliance.summary: Free education from early childhood through to tertiary level.

vision-nz.summary: An inquiry into falling standards, political neutrality in classrooms, and higher teacher pay.

issues.title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and Māori issues
issues.why_it_matters: How the Treaty of Waitangi is applied in law has been one of the most debated questions of this term. Some parties want to limit Treaty clauses in law and programmes targeted by ethnicity (which they call 'race-based'); others want Te Tiriti given more legal weight. The future of the Māori seats and the Waitangi Tribunal is also on the ballot.

key_facts.fact: ACT's Treaty Principles Bill was voted down 112 to 11 at its second reading on 10 April 2025; only ACT voted for it.
305,124 Māori voters were on the Māori roll and 255,900 on the general roll (54.4% on the Māori roll) as of 3 August 2026.
Voters rated Te Pāti Māori as the party most capable on Māori issues (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: Voted against the Treaty Principles Bill; in the Herald leaders' debate (14 Oct 2026) Luxon said he was willing to consider backing a referendum on the Māori seats.

labour.summary: Restore Te Tiriti obligations on school boards, restore iwi participation agreements in resource management, and direct 5% of government contracts to Māori businesses.

green.summary: Entrench the Māori seats, uphold Te Tiriti across government, $200 million for te reo Māori, and a trust to support marae.

act.summary: Scale back Treaty principles in law, remove ethnicity-based criteria from public services, and abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved.

nz-first.summary: A binding referendum on the Māori seats, abolish Auckland's Independent Māori Statutory Board, and replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty completion commission.

te-pati-maori.summary: An independent Te Tiriti Commission, binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations, a Māori constitutional convention (Matike Mai) and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in practice.

opportunity.summary: Teach Te Tiriti and Aotearoa history in schools, restore pre-2025 customary marine title settings, and not support a Treaty Principles bill.

te-tai-tokerau-party.summary: Constitutionally protect He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti, repeal the Regulatory Standards Act, and make Waitangi Tribunal findings binding on the Crown.

conservative.summary: 'One people under one law': opposes policies that treat people differently by race or ancestry.

vision-nz.summary: End race-based policies and policies it links to the He Puapua report.

issues.title: Infrastructure and transport
issues.why_it_matters: Roads, rail, water pipes, hospitals and schools all need fixing or building; planned projects are valued at about $275 billion. Much of what is planned has no money set aside yet. Parties differ on roads versus public transport and on how to pay.

key_facts.fact: New Zealand spends over $20 billion a year on infrastructure but gets less for its money than many similar countries (Infrastructure Commission).
Nearly 12,000 planned infrastructure projects are worth about $275 billion, but more than two-thirds don't yet have full funding.
Economist Cameron Bagrie says every major party is offering too little for roads by not raising fuel taxes, warning of a 'gaping hole' by about 2028.

national.summary: Finish the next Roads of National Significance, fund the $800 million Christchurch Northern Motorway extension, finish Auckland's Eastern Busway and remove Auckland level crossings.

labour.summary: Cap public transport fares, spend more on fixing schools and hospitals, and restore cancelled rural school bus routes.

green.summary: Mass rapid transit in the three biggest cities, new intercity passenger rail (about $4 billion), removing Auckland level crossings, and $2 fares.

act.summary: Spend the land transport fund on roads only and require projects to consider a cheaper option.

nz-first.summary: A 12-month commuter rail trial in Canterbury and further south, and make fast-tracked housing include roads and water infrastructure.

opportunity.summary: A funded 30-year infrastructure plan, up to $60 billion of borrowing for it, 60% of spending on maintenance and renewals, and free public transport.

alliance.summary: Public ownership of rail and key ports, and a new Ministry of Works to build infrastructure.

vision-nz.summary: Build roads that cut congestion and commuting times.

issues.title: Immigration
issues.why_it_matters: More New Zealand citizens are leaving than returning, while migrant arrivals have risen. Some parties want tighter rules on visas, benefits and citizenship. Others want easier paths to residency and family visas.

key_facts.fact: Net migration added 20,500 people in the year to August 2026, about double the year before but below the long-run average.
New Zealand citizens had a net loss of 38,200 people (64,800 left long-term, 26,600 came home), while non-citizens had a net gain of 58,800.
59% of people in a Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll favoured limiting general-election voting to citizens; 32% were opposed (August 2026).

national.summary: Fast-track visas for partners of New Zealand citizens, encourage wealthy investor visa holders to stay, and make new residents wait five years for benefits; keeps the permanent resident visa.

labour.summary: A citizenship pathway for children of migrants born here, let migrants move between accredited employers, a four-year path to permanent residence, and wider visa-free travel for Pacific Islands Forum countries.

green.summary: A pathway to residency for migrant workers, a higher refugee quota, help for migrant families to get visas, and more visa-free travel for Pacific visitors.

act.summary: Deport serious non-citizen offenders, a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, stronger English requirements, a physical-presence test for residents, and a Rural Workforce Visa.

nz-first.summary: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led visa, remove automatic work rights for students, a 10-year benefit stand-down for migrants, a two-year amnesty for overstayers who leave, and higher citizenship fees.

conservative.summary: Shift visas away from unskilled workers towards skilled professionals and entrepreneurs using a stable points system.

vision-nz.summary: Pause what it calls 'mass immigration' and extend the wait for citizenship to 10 years.

issues.title: Superannuation and retirement
issues.why_it_matters: NZ Super is paid to almost everyone from age 65 and its cost is rising fast as the population ages. Several parties want to change KiwiSaver to boost savings. Others want to change who qualifies for NZ Super, or when.

key_facts.fact: NZ Super costs $24.7 billion this financial year (2025/26) and is forecast to reach $31.2 billion in 2029/30 (Budget 2026).
The government is forecast to put $3.1 billion into the NZ Superannuation Fund over the next four years; withdrawals are expected from 2054.

national.summary: Make KiwiSaver compulsory and enrol babies at birth with a $1,500 'Baby Boost', and require retirement villages to repay departing residents within nine months.

labour.summary: Make employer KiwiSaver contributions compulsory, more flexible KiwiSaver for workers, and make retirement villages repay residents within three months.

green.summary: Return to a 10-year residency requirement for NZ Super and create a state-owned retirement village system.

act.summary: Raise the NZ Super age gradually to 67 by 2035, stop taxing KiwiSaver earnings, and keep payments into the NZ Super Fund suspended.

nz-first.summary: Pay NZ Super only to citizens and enrol every newborn citizen in KiwiSaver.

opportunity.summary: Gradually raise KiwiSaver contributions to 6% and make it compulsory; its Citizen's Income would replace current benefits.

alliance.summary: Keep NZ Super universal, raise the couple rate to the legal maximum, end the asset test for rest-home care, and give new KiwiSaver accounts a $10,000 start.

conservative.summary: Stop taxing NZ Super, including for people who keep working after 65.

issues.title: Farming and rural New Zealand
issues.why_it_matters: Farming, food and forestry earn most of New Zealand's export income. Farmers face rules on water, emissions and land use that parties want to loosen or tighten. Rural communities also care about workers, water storage and services.

key_facts.fact: Food and fibre exports were forecast at a record $64.3 billion for the year to June 2026, up 6% (MPI Situation and Outlook, June 2026).
Agriculture produces about half of New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions, and farm emissions are not priced in the emissions trading scheme.

national.summary: Keep farm emissions out of the ETS, $300 million of low-cost loans for water storage, national standards for everyday farm activities, and more places on the vet bonding scheme.

labour.summary: Review the emissions trading scheme, including how it affects farming.

green.summary: Phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, cap nitrogen use, ban imported palm kernel feed, and reduce farm emissions.

act.summary: Keep farming out of emissions programmes, a three-year Rural Workforce Visa, accept trusted overseas approvals for farm chemicals, and let routine farm work go ahead without resource consent.

nz-first.summary: Guarantee more milk for New Zealand dairy manufacturers and help small food suppliers get onto supermarket shelves.

te-pati-maori.summary: Protect Māori food systems and support on-farm and rural energy generation.

opportunity.summary: Bring farming into a strengthened emissions trading scheme and rewrite gene technology rules.

animal-justice.summary: A farmer-led national programme with transition planning, financial help and debt restructuring for farmers moving to plant-based or other land uses.

conservative.summary: Oppose converting farmland to carbon forestry and oppose the Gene Technology Bill.

issues.title: Foreign affairs, trade and defence
issues.why_it_matters: War in the Middle East and tension in the Pacific have made foreign policy a bigger issue than usual. New Zealand is spending more on defence and signing new trade deals. Parties disagree on Israel and Palestine, AUKUS, foreign aid and military alliances.

key_facts.fact: The 2025 Defence Capability Plan commits $12 billion over four years ($9 billion new) and aims to lift defence spending from just over 1% to more than 2% of GDP within eight years.
New Zealand's free trade agreement with India came into force on 20 October 2026.
Voters rated National as most capable on defence and foreign affairs (Ipsos, Sept 2026).

national.summary: Pursue trade deals with Europe, South America, Asia and Africa, cut foreign aid outside the Pacific to fund medicines, and ratify the High Seas Biodiversity Treaty.

labour.summary: Recognise a Palestinian state, raise foreign aid to 0.7% of GDP, not join AUKUS, and support the India trade deal with conditions.

green.summary: Recognise Palestine and sanction Israel, rewrite foreign policy to oppose imperialism, and refuse to buy autonomous weapons.

act.summary: Cut foreign aid back to 2017 levels and renegotiate New Zealand's Paris Agreement commitment, or leave it.

nz-first.summary: Protect New Zealand-made aluminium with trade barriers; it opposed the India trade deal, calling it "a bad deal for New Zealand" that "gives too much away, especially on immigration".

te-pati-maori.summary: Declare New Zealand militarily neutral, focus the Defence Force on disaster response and the Pacific, and hold war criminals to account.

free-palestine.summary: A single democratic state in Palestine and an independent foreign policy, withdrawing from military and security alliances with the US.

alliance.summary: A non-aligned foreign policy centred on the Pacific, support for a strong United Nations and disarmament, and an end to US military and intelligence facilities in New Zealand.

nz-loyal.summary: End New Zealand's participation in the UN, WEF and WHO.

vision-nz.summary: Suspend New Zealand's commitment to UN regulations and leave the Paris Accord.

conservative.summary: Review all trade agreements and pursue a neutral foreign policy, with a military focused on support and reconstruction.

nz-outdoors-freedom.summary: Leave the CPTPP and RCEP trade agreements and pursue 'fair trade' deals country by country.

issues.title: Democracy and how government works
issues.why_it_matters: Several parties want to change how elections and Parliament work, from voting rules to political donations. This is the first election since 2017 at which you cannot enrol on election day. Some proposals would change who can vote or how MPs are elected.

key_facts.fact: You can no longer enrol on election day: enrolment for the 2026 election closes on 25 October 2026, before advance voting starts on 26 October.
Turnout at the 2023 election was 78.2% of enrolled voters.
17 parties are registered to contest the 2026 party vote.

national.summary: Hold referendums on the MMP voting system and on moving to a four-year parliamentary term, and set up an election policy costings unit.

labour.summary: Restore same-day enrolment, let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in local elections, repeal the Regulatory Standards Act, a lobbying register, and an independent body to cost party policies.

green.summary: Cap political donations at $30,000 and ban company donations, regulate lobbying, expand voting rights, and entrench the Māori seats.

act.summary: Merge government departments and cut ministers, and remove voting rights from unelected council appointees.

nz-first.summary: Only citizens could vote, and a binding referendum on the Māori seats.

te-pati-maori.summary: An independent Commissioner for Te Tiriti o Waitangi to scrutinise laws.

opportunity.summary: Citizens' assemblies for major decisions, a $30,000 donation cap, a lobbying register and a political corruption watchdog.

nz-outdoors-freedom.summary: Direct democracy through binding citizen votes, and make the Bill of Rights supreme law.

vision-nz.summary: Abolish MMP party lists so only electorate winners sit in Parliament, cut the number of MPs, and add term limits for MPs.

animal-justice.summary: Get money out of politics and protect whistleblowers.

nz-loyal.summary: Write a New Zealand constitution and decentralise government.

alliance.summary: Lower the MMP threshold to 3.5% and hold a public review towards a written constitution grounded in Te Tiriti.

howtovote._about: How to vote in the 7 November 2026 New Zealand general election. Plain-English guide for Ballot Book NZ. Every fact is tied to the Electoral Commission page (vote.nz / elections.nz), the Act, or the news report it came from, with the date the source was retrieved. Commission pages were fetched with a headless browser on 23 October 2026 (copies in raw/howtovote/). Where a fact could not be verified against a primary source, the text says so. This guide is not legal advice: if your situation is unusual, call the Electoral Commission on 0800 36 76 56.

election.name: 2026 General Election
election.election_day_text: Saturday 7 November 2026, voting places open 9am to 7pm
election.law_change_note: In December 2025 Parliament passed the Electoral Amendment Act 2025, which (Public Act 2025 No 82, Royal assent 19 December 2025, most of it in force from 20 December 2025). It closes enrolment 13 days before election day, so there is no enrolling at a voting place during advance voting or on election day; sets a 12-day advance voting period; and bars more sentenced prisoners from voting. Sources: Ministry of Justice summary (justice.govt.nz, retrieved 23 Oct 2026); RNZ, 'Electoral Amendment Bill passes its third reading in Parliament' (Dec 2025); Electoral Act 1993 as at 1 January 2026, s 3(1) 'close of registration', s 80, s 171B.

key_dates.event: Last day for Māori already enrolled to change between the Māori roll and the general roll (midnight). You can't change rolls in the 3 months before an election.
Writ Day. If you were enrolled by this date you get an EasyVote card and are on the printed roll. Anyone who enrols or updates after this date casts a special vote.
Registration opens for telephone dictation voting (0800 028 028, option 1).
EasyVote cards start going out by email and post (delivery 14 to 22 October).
Last recommended day to post a paper enrolment form (Tuesday). Forms arriving by post after Tuesday 27 October cannot be accepted.
Overseas voting and telephone dictation voting start (Wednesday).
ENROLMENT CLOSES at midnight (Sunday). This is the last moment to enrol or update your address. No enrolling at voting places this election.
Advance voting starts in New Zealand (Monday, Labour Day). Hours vary by place. 207 voting places open on the first day.
Last day of advance voting (Friday). Regulated period for election advertising ends; all election advertising must stop and signs come down by midnight.

ELECTION DAY (Saturday). Voting places open 9am to 7pm. Telephone dictation registration closes at noon; dictation voting, overseas uploads and all voting close at 7pm NZ time. Preliminary results from 7pm on electionresults.govt.nz.
Official results declared (Friday), after special votes are checked and counted and every vote is recounted.
Last day for the return of the writ (the formal list of elected electorate MPs). The new Parliament's three-year term runs from this date.
Latest date Parliament must meet (6 weeks after the day fixed for the return of the writ, Constitution Act 1986 s 19). RNZ's The House gives the date as 14 January.

contacts.electoral_commission_freephone: 0800 36 76 56 (free, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; enrolment questions, finding a voting place, help to vote)
contacts.text_for_an_enrolment_form: Text your name and address to 3676 (free) and a form is posted to you
contacts.enrolment_email: enrol@vote.nz (to return a scanned or photographed enrolment form)
contacts.enrol_or_check_online: https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/enrol-or-update-online (needs a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity)
contacts.post: Electoral Commission, FREEPOST 2 ENROL, PO Box 190, Wellington 6140
contacts.general_enquiries_email: enquiries@elections.govt.nz (questions, complaints about election advertising or misleading voting information)
contacts.telephone_dictation: 0800 028 028 within NZ (option 1 to register, option 2 to vote); +64 4 471 2000 from overseas
contacts.electorate_managers: https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/contact-your-electorate-manager (name, email and phone for each electorate; use this if you can't get to a voting place)

checklist.done_when: You are 18 or older on election day, a NZ citizen or a resident for electoral purposes (your visa doesn't make you leave by a set date), and you have lived in NZ continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life. If you are 17 now but turn 18 by 7 November, you can enrol.

checklist.step: Check you are enrolled at your current address, before midnight Sunday 25 October
checklist.done_when: The online check at vote.nz shows your name and current address (you need a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe), or you have called 0800 36 76 56 and been told you are enrolled. After midnight 25 October nothing can be changed and you cannot enrol at a voting place.

checklist.step: Pick where and when you will vote
checklist.done_when: You have looked up a voting place and its hours on the official map (hours vary before election day), or you know a place that is open 9am to 7pm on Saturday 7 November. You can vote at any voting place in NZ, but it is quicker close to home.

checklist.step: Know what to bring: nothing is required
checklist.done_when: You know no ID is needed. If you have an EasyVote card (sent to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email or post) bring it on paper, on your phone or as a screenshot; it makes finding you on the roll faster.

You know you make one tick on the left for a party (party vote) and one tick on the right for a local candidate (electorate vote). One tick for each. You may do just one side if you want. If you make a mistake, ask for a new paper.

checklist.step: Plan ahead if you will be away or overseas
checklist.done_when: Away from home in NZ: you know you can vote at any voting place (you will fill in a short special-vote declaration). Overseas on or after 21 October: you know you must be enrolled by 25 October, then download your papers at vote.nz/overseas, sign the declaration with a witness, and upload by 7pm NZ time on 7 November.

checklist.step: Get help if you need it
checklist.done_when: You know a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read the paper and mark it as you ask (they can't tell you who to vote for). If you are blind, have low vision or a physical disability, you have registered for telephone dictation voting (0800 028 028) by noon on 7 November. If you can't get to a voting place, you have called 0800 36 76 56 or your electorate manager.

voting_places.deep_link_notes: The official finder (map.vote.nz, redirects to map.vote.nz/voting-places) is a client-side map. It loads the whole 2026 voting-place dataset into the browser and filters it there, with an address search box (Mapbox geocoding) and filters for day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua. It takes no documented URL parameters: on 23 Oct 2026 we tested https://map.vote.nz/voting-places?electorate=Wellington%20Central and the page loaded the default view. The vote.nz list page lets you pick an electorate and suburb from drop-downs, also client-side. So the app should deep-link to https://map.vote.nz and let the voter type their address, or call 0800 36 76 56. Posters listing nearby voting places are also displayed at local supermarkets and community libraries during advance voting.
voting_places.data_endpoint: https://map.vote.nz/assets/map-data/locations-<hash>.json (the hash changes when the data is updated; on 23 Oct 2026 it was a 1.05 MB JSON file with 2,641 locations, each with name, address, suburb, WGS84 coordinates, accessibility code (none/partial/full), Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua flags, per-day opening hours, and the electorates it serves as a 'Home' or 'Shared' place). It is served from behind the Commission's bot protection (Incapsula) and is not published on data.govt.nz.
voting_places.licence: No licence statement was found on the data file, on map.vote.nz, or on vote.nz/elections.nz (their footers say only 'Copyright © Electoral Commission New Zealand'). Because there is no licence allowing reuse, the dataset is NOT stored in this repository; only the deep-link above is published. tools/howtovote_voting_places.py can normalise the file if the Commission confirms reuse terms (enquiries@elections.govt.nz). For 2023 the Commission published a 'voting place coordinates' CSV on the results archive (archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/statistics/) marked 'approximate only', again with no licence stated.
voting_places.when_published: The Commission announced the 2026 voting places on 7 October 2026 ('about 3 weeks before election day' is its stated practice). Hours and places can still change, so always check the finder before travelling.

counts_from_commission.fact: More than 2,300 voting places open on election day (the finder data held 2,314 on 23 Oct); 207 open on Monday 26 October (finder data: 209) offering 1,437 hours of voting; the number grows towards election day.

1,679 fully accessible voting places; NZ Sign Language interpreters at six locations; three voting places with quiet times; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori voting places (marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces), including 67 bilingual (reo rua) places where you can vote in te reo Māori or English.
Votes will be taken at 2,638 locations across the whole voting period (RNZ, citing the Commission).

sections.title: 1. Am I allowed to vote?
who_its_for: people in prison or on remand

steps.text: You can enrol and vote if all three are true: you are 18 or older; you are a New Zealand citizen or a 'resident for electoral purposes'; and you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life.
steps.source: vote.nz, 'Are you eligible to enrol and vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 74

steps.text: 'Resident for electoral purposes' means you live in New Zealand lawfully and your visa does not make you leave by a set date. Resident-visa holders (including the 2021 Resident Visa) qualify. People on work, student or visitor visas with an end date do not.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: If you are 17 you can fill in the form now. You are enrolled automatically on your 18th birthday. If you turn 18 on or before 7 November 2026, you can vote, as long as you applied to enrol by midnight 25 October.
steps.source: vote.nz EasyVote page and eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: If you live in New Zealand and are eligible, enrolling is compulsory by law. Voting itself is not compulsory.
steps.source: vote.nz, 'Need help to vote?' (dementia section) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Prison (changed in 2025): you cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of 3 years or more. You also cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of less than 3 years for any offence committed on or after 20 December 2025. You CAN still vote if you are serving less than 3 years and all your offences happened before 20 December 2025, or if you are on remand, home detention or a community sentence. The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting for eligible prisoners.
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 80(1)(d) as at 1 Jan 2026 (raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); Ministry of Justice, 'Electoral law changes'

steps.text: You also cannot vote if you are a NZ citizen who has not been in New Zealand in the last 3 years, a resident (non-citizen) who has not been in NZ in the last 12 months, if you have been held in a psychiatric hospital for more than 3 years after a criminal charge, or if you are on the Corrupt Practices List.
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80

steps.text: Homeless? You can enrol at the address where you spend most of your time, or the last address where you lived for a month or more. You need a postal address (a PO Box or a friend, family member, church or support group who will hold mail for you).
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: The brief said 'prisoners now barred under the 2025 Act'. Verified with a correction: the ban is not total. Sentenced prisoners serving under 3 years can still vote if all their offences were before 20 December 2025 (Electoral Act s 80(1)(d)(i)-(ii); vote.nz). RNZ (Dec 2025) reported the Act 'bans prisoners from voting'; 1News (16 Oct 2026) called it 'a total ban on prisoner voting for prisoners sentenced after December 2025'. The Act's wording turns on when the offence happened, not the sentencing date.
Unsure? Call 0800 36 76 56. The law is Electoral Act 1993 ss 74 and 80.

sections.title: 2. Enrol or update your details by midnight, Sunday 25 October

steps.text: Deadline: midnight, Sunday 25 October 2026. The law now closes the roll 13 days before election day. You cannot enrol or change your address after this, and you cannot enrol at a voting place during advance voting or on election day. Voting place staff can't make exceptions; the rule is set by law.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' and eligibility pages, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 3(1) 'close of registration' (inserted by Electoral Amendment Act 2025 s 4(2)); 1News 16 Oct 2026 ('there are no exceptions, the Electoral Commission says')

steps.text: Fastest way: online at vote.nz with your NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity. The same page lets you check what address you are enrolled at.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 22 Oct 2026

steps.text: No ID? Fill in the form online and have it emailed or posted to you to sign ('Enrol without ID' / 'Update without ID'), download the PDF form, call 0800 36 76 56, or text your name and address to 3676. Then return the signed form by upload (vote.nz/upload), email (enrol@vote.nz), or drop it at an enrolment hub. Hub times and places are at vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/enrolment-in-your-community.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Post is slow: the Commission recommended posting forms by Tuesday 20 October. It will accept forms that arrive by post on Tuesday 27 October but not after. If you still have a paper form, upload or email it, or take it to a hub.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Moved house but still enrolled at an old address? You can still vote, but you may need to cast a special vote. If your new home is in a different electorate, only your party vote will count. Update your address by 25 October so both votes count.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23
