steps.text: Dormant roll: if mail from the Commission came back from your old address you may be on the 'dormant roll'. You can still vote (as a special vote) but, again, if you have moved electorate only your party vote counts. Updating your address before 25 October fixes this.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Not enrolled at any address by midnight 25 October? The Commission says you will not be able to vote in this election. If you turn up believing you are enrolled, you can cast a special vote, but it will be disallowed if you turn out not to be enrolled.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23; 1News 16 Oct 2026

steps.text: Unpublished roll: if you fear for your safety, you can ask to go on the confidential unpublished roll (download the form or call 0800 36 76 56). Your details are kept off printed rolls. You will then cast a special vote, you can't check or update your details online, and you can't download overseas voting papers.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Māori roll or general roll: if you are of Māori descent you choose a roll when you first enrol. You vote for the same parties on either roll; the difference is which electorate candidates you choose from. Already-enrolled Māori could change rolls until midnight 6 August 2026; the 3-month pre-election freeze now applies. If you are enrolling for the first time you can still choose either roll up to 25 October.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates and 'Māori roll or general roll?'; Electoral Commission release '17,000 Māori voters change rolls', 18 Aug 2026

notes: Why it changed: the Government said late enrolments put 'too much strain on the system' and slowed the count (Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, quoted by RNZ, July 2025). The Attorney-General reported the cut-off 'appears to constitute an unjustified limit' on the right to vote under the Bill of Rights Act (reported by RNZ). The Chief Electoral Officer told MPs the change was 'not a change that we recommended' and would not make official results faster than 20 days (RNZ, Sept 2025). Labour has said it would reverse the change (RNZ). Both sides' views are reported here; the guide takes no position.

Scale: in 2023, about 450,000 people enrolled or updated in the final two weeks, including about 110,000 on election day (1News, 16 Oct 2026, citing Commission data). The Commission expects about 55,000 special votes to be disallowed this year, five times more than usual, because the voter turns out not to be enrolled (1News).
On 21 October 2026, 3,729,667 people were enrolled, 92.1% of those eligible; only 68.6% of 18 to 24 year olds were enrolled (Electoral Commission, 22 Oct 2026).

Enrolment packs were posted 17 to 22 August 2026; if you didn't get one, your address was out of date or you were not enrolled (Electoral Commission, 10 Aug 2026). The Commission also used data matching with NZTA and Internal Affairs to contact 170,000 people in September (release 17 Sep 2026).

sections.title: 3. When and where to vote

steps.text: Advance voting: Monday 26 October to Friday 6 November. You can vote at any voting place in New Zealand. Days and hours differ from place to place, and some places open only before election day or only on election day, so check before you go.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find a voting place', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 171B (12-day advance period)

steps.text: Election day: Saturday 7 November, every voting place open 9am to 7pm. If you are inside a voting place at 7pm waiting to vote, you can still vote.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates; Electoral Act s 161

steps.text: Find a place: use the official map at map.vote.nz (search your address; filter by day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori, reo rua), the list by electorate and suburb on vote.nz, posters at your local supermarket or library, or call 0800 36 76 56.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find a voting place'; Electoral Commission releases 7 and 22 Oct 2026

steps.text: Vote close to home if you can. It is faster because your name is on the printed roll there. Anywhere else you can still vote, but you fill in a special-vote declaration first.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: What to bring: nothing. No ID is needed. Bring your EasyVote card if you have one (paper, phone or screenshot); it helps staff find you on the roll. You can vote without it.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections' ('No ID is required') and EasyVote page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: EasyVote cards went to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email (from no-reply@easy.vote.nz; follow-up texts from 5101) or by post, between 14 and 22 October. Check your spam folder. If you enrolled after 4 October you won't get one, but you can still vote.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release, 14 Oct 2026; vote.nz EasyVote page

steps.text: Quieter times: if you prefer less crowding or need assistance, the Commission says 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays are usually best.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Time off work on election day: if you haven't had a reasonable chance to vote before starting work, your employer must let you leave by 3pm for the rest of the day, with no pay docked. If you do essential work after 3pm, you get a reasonable time off earlier in the day, with up to 2 hours paid. Employers who refuse can be fined up to $1,000.
steps.source: Electoral Act 1993 s 162 (verified in the consolidated Act as at 1 Jan 2026, raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?' (time away from work section)

notes: Staff wear orange vests and will guide you. Many are working their first election; the Commission asks for patience if there are delays (vote.nz, 'What to expect at the voting place').
Monday 26 October is Labour Day; 207 voting places open that day (Commission release 22 Oct 2026; RNZ explainer 23 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 4. Voting away from home, special votes, and voting when you can't get to a voting place
who_its_for: students and workers away from home
people on the unpublished or dormant roll
people in hospital, care homes or prison
people with illness or mobility problems

steps.text: A special vote is a normal vote plus a short declaration form you sign. You cast one if your name is not on the printed roll where you vote: because you enrolled or updated after Writ Day (4 October), you are voting outside your electorate, you are on the unpublished roll, you are on the dormant roll, or you are voting from overseas or away from a voting place.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do'; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; Electoral Act s 61

steps.text: Voting in another electorate: you get the ballot paper for YOUR home electorate, so your electorate vote still counts, as long as you are enrolled there. If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in, the electorate vote is disallowed and only your party vote is counted ('Party Vote Only').
steps.source: elections.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: How special votes are counted: they are sent back to your home electorate, every declaration is checked against the roll, and they are added to the official count. They can arrive up to 10 days after election day. That is why they are not in election-night results and why official results take until 27 November.
steps.source: elections.nz; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?'

steps.text: Can't get to a voting place (illness, mobility)? Someone can collect your voting papers for you ('takeaway' voting). Sign a written authorisation (form on vote.nz, or handwritten with your name, phone, enrolled address, which roll you are on, and a line authorising the bearer). They bring the papers to you; you complete them with a witnessed special-vote declaration; they must be back at a voting place before 7pm on 7 November.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Nobody to collect them? Contact your electorate manager (list on vote.nz). It may be possible for papers to be delivered to you and collected again.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In hospital: a friend or family member can bring you your voting papers. If you know you will be in hospital, the Commission suggests voting in advance. In a care home or rest home: you don't need to do anything; the electorate manager arranges voting with your home's manager. Ask your home what has been arranged.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Blind, low vision or a physical disability that stops you marking the paper: use telephone dictation voting (see Accessibility section). Remote locations (DOC islands, offshore installations, vessels in NZ waters): apply early to remote@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Remote voting', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In prison or on remand and eligible? The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting services.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: The Commission forecast around 700,000 special votes for 2026 (Chief Electoral Officer to the Justice Committee, RNZ, Sept 2025). In 2023 there were 603,257 special votes, 20.9% of all votes (Commission, 3 Nov 2023).

'Voting from home' in the sense of postal voting for everyone does not exist for general elections in New Zealand; the options above (collected papers, electorate-manager delivery, dictation, remote and overseas services) are what the Commission offers.

sections.title: 5. Voting from overseas
who_its_for: Defence Force and public servants posted overseas

steps.text: Who can: you must be enrolled, 18+, have lived in NZ for 12+ continuous months at some time, and be either a NZ citizen who has been in NZ within the last 3 years, or a resident for electoral purposes who has been in NZ within the last 12 months. Public servants, diplomats and Defence Force members posted overseas, and their families, qualify however long they have been away. Enrolling from overseas is optional.
steps.source: vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80(1)(a)-(b)

steps.text: Enrol or update by midnight Sunday 25 October, NZ time. You can't download papers until your enrolment is processed, so do it early. Your electorate is where you last lived for a month or more. If you have been away too long to update online, email overseas@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Voting opened Wednesday 21 October (NZ time). The easiest way: download your papers at vote.nz/overseas (a 3-page PDF: instructions, declaration, ballot paper), mark them on screen or print and mark by hand, then upload them. You must be physically outside New Zealand when you download; if you download while still in NZ your vote will not be counted.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Downloading your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: The declaration must be signed by you AND a witness who is physically with you. Typed signatures and handwriting-style fonts are not accepted; draw or insert an image of your real signature. Tick your reason for a special vote (e.g. outside NZ on election day). Your witness can be a relative, flatmate, colleague or associate, any registered NZ elector, or an official such as a notary.
steps.source: vote.nz 'How to complete your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Upload at uvp.elections.govt.nz by 7pm on Saturday 7 November, NZ time. Late papers cannot be accepted. Upload once only: more than one submission may mean your vote doesn't count. Files: JPG, PNG, GIF, PDF or TIFF, 10 KB to 10 MB, whole page visible including the 7-digit number top right.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Uploading your voting papers', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In person: 64 overseas locations offer in-person or postal voting, including 10 in Australia. Hours and closing dates differ, some are appointment-only or postal-only, most are closed at weekends, and ALL overseas voting places are closed on election day, 7 November. Check the lookup before you go.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find an overseas voting place'; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026

steps.text: On the unpublished roll? You can't download papers. Ask your nearest overseas voting place for a postal vote or collect papers in person, or email overseas@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Help: overseas@vote.nz or +64 9 909 4182. Blind or disabled voters overseas can use telephone dictation voting on +64 4 471 2000 (register first).
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: In 2023, 88% of overseas voters used the download service; 77,295 overseas votes were received (62,787 in 2020). About 126,000 enrolled voters have told the Commission they live overseas, 64% of them in Australia (Electoral Commission, 21 Oct 2026).
Niueans, Tokelauans and Cook Islanders vote on the citizen rule (in NZ within 3 years); Australians on the resident rule (within 12 months) (vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas').
The brief's 'from 21 Oct?' is confirmed: overseas voting started Wednesday 21 October 2026 (vote.nz key dates; Commission release 21 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 6. Help to vote and accessible voting
who_its_for: people with dementia or cognitive impairment

steps.text: A support person: a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read out the paper, and mark it as you ask. They cannot tell you who to vote for. The choice must be yours and you must be present. Nobody can vote for you, not even with power of attorney.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 170

steps.text: Telephone dictation voting is for people who are blind, partially blind or have a physical disability that stops them marking the paper. You must register every election, even if you used it before. Register from Monday 5 October to noon on Saturday 7 November by calling 0800 028 028 (option 1) or +64 4 471 2000 from overseas. Registration hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm; from 26 October also Saturdays 9am to 3pm; election day 9am to noon.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Telephone dictation voting', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Then vote by phone from Wednesday 21 October to 7pm on Saturday 7 November (0800 028 028, option 2). You give your registration number and the answer to a secret question, not your name. One official reads out the candidates and parties and marks your paper; a second official checks it back with you. Dictation voting hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm, Saturdays 9am to 3pm (from 26 Oct), election day 9am to 7pm.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026

steps.text: Accessible voting places: 1,679 are fully accessible; NZSL interpreters are at six locations; three places have quiet times. The map at map.vote.nz can be filtered by accessibility.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026; vote.nz 'Find a voting place'

steps.text: Information in other formats: audio, Braille, large print, Easy Read and New Zealand Sign Language (NZSL) versions of the enrolling and voting guides are at vote.nz. Easy Read: 'Get ready to enrol and vote in the 2026 General Election' (PDF). Most vote.nz pages also have te reo Māori and NZSL versions (language toggle at the top).
steps.source: vote.nz 'Information in accessible formats' and 'Information in Easy Read', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Access 2026 is the Commission's accessibility action plan: 20 accessible services for Deaf and disabled people, tāngata Turi (Deaf Māori) and tāngata whaikaha Māori (disabled Māori), with Easy Read, large print, audio and Braille summaries.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Sep 2026; elections.nz Access 2026 page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Dementia or cognitive impairment: there is no capacity test for voting. A person can vote if they want to and can clearly show their choice at the time; a support person must follow their instructions.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Te reo Māori: 67 bilingual (reo rua) voting places let you vote in te reo Māori or English; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori places are at marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces. Filter the map for 'Whare Pōti Māori' and 'Reo rua'.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026

notes: Quiet times at voting places are generally 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays (vote.nz).

The Access 2026 'Quick guide to accessible voting services' PDF could not be downloaded (bot protection); its contents are summarised from the Access 2026 web page and the telephone dictation page instead.
Disabled voters told 1News (5 Oct 2026, cited in docs/FEATURE_REVIEW.md) they were still hunting for accessible booths; the map's accessibility filter and 0800 36 76 56 are the Commission's answers.

sections.title: 7. First time voting? What happens inside, and the two ticks

steps.text: Arrive. Staff in orange vests greet you. Give your EasyVote card, or your name and address, to the person issuing papers. They find you on the roll (electronic roll for dormant-roll voters) and hand you your voting paper. If you are not on the printed roll you fill in a special-vote declaration first.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to expect' and 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Go to a voting screen and vote in private, with a pen. You get two votes on one paper. LEFT side: your party vote. Tick ONE circle next to the party you want in government. RIGHT side: your electorate vote. Tick ONE circle next to the candidate you want as the MP for your area.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: You can tick both sides, or just one side. Both are valid. The party vote decides how many seats each party gets in Parliament; the electorate vote picks your local MP. Your EasyVote card comes with the list of candidates for your electorate; party lists are on vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' ('vote for only one or the other, it's your choice'); elections.nz 'What happens in a general election?'

steps.text: Made a mistake? Take the 'spoilt' paper back and ask for a new one. Spoilt papers are not counted. An 'informal' vote is one where the counters cannot tell what you intended; it is recorded but does not count. If your intention is clear, your vote counts even if the paper has been drawn on.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' (spoilt papers) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections' (informal votes), retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Fold the paper in half and put it in the ballot box. Then leave; the Commission asks voters not to linger so others feel comfortable.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' and 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Phones and selfies: don't film or photograph inside a voting place. Publishing a photo or video of someone filling in their paper is a potential offence. Candidates who want to be filmed voting must arrange it in advance (returns@elections.govt.nz / the Returning Officer).
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to expect'; Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (PDF, 2026)

steps.text: Campaigning near voting places: during advance voting, no campaigning, election advertising or influencing voters inside a voting place or within 10 metres of its entrance. On election day those rules apply everywhere until 7pm: no campaign material (a lapel badge or rosette is allowed), no processions, no polling voters. New in 2026: nobody may give out free food, drink (except water) or entertainment within 100 metres of a voting place entrance while voting is open, unless it is their normal business.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (raw/howtovote/rules-once-voting-starts.pdf); Ministry of Justice summary of the 2025 Act

steps.text: Social media on election day: from midnight before election day until 7pm on 7 November, you must not post or share anything likely to influence someone's party or candidate vote. There is no exemption for personal opinions online on election day. Posts made before election day can stay up if not updated. Paid election advertising online is banned on election day.
steps.source: elections.nz 'Social media' and vote.nz 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Scrutineers: you may see people with party rosettes sitting along one side. They are appointed by candidates and parties to watch, not Commission staff, and they cannot talk to voters.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: Votes are counted by hand; New Zealand does not use voting machines (vote.nz, 'Facts about New Zealand elections').

Who to vote for is your decision. This guide does not recommend anyone. RNZ's 23 Oct 2026 explainer points first-time voters to non-partisan candidate information at policy.nz and the parties' own websites.

If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in (e.g. you moved and didn't update), only your party vote counts (elections.nz, 'Party Vote Only'). In 2023 more than 42,000 electorate votes were disallowed for this reason; the Commission estimated more than 72,000 could be this year (1News, 16 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 8. After you vote: results and forming a government

steps.text: Election night: advance votes are counted from 9am on election day at electorate headquarters; election-day votes are counted at each voting place after 7pm. Preliminary results go up progressively from 7pm on electionresults.govt.nz. The Commission's targets: 50% of results by 10pm and 95% by 11.30pm.
steps.source: elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Election-night results are NOT final. They leave out all special votes (including overseas votes) and the rolls have not yet been checked. The Commission says they 'are likely to change'.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Special votes have changed results before. 2023: after specials, National went from 50 seats to 48, Te Pāti Māori from 4 to 6, the Greens from 14 to 15; Nelson, Te Atatū, Tāmaki Makaurau (by 4 votes) and Te Tai Tokerau changed hands; National and ACT alone no longer had a majority. 603,257 special votes were 20.9% of the total.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, 'Official results for the 2023 General Election', 3 Nov 2023

steps.text: 2020: National fell from 35 seats to 33, Labour rose from 64 to 65 and the Māori Party from 1 to 2; Maungakiekie, Northland and Whangārei switched from National to Labour. 504,625 special votes were 17% of the total.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, '2020 General Election official results', 6 Nov 2020

steps.text: Official results: Friday 27 November 2026 (20 days after election day). Every vote is recounted by hand, special votes (which can arrive up to 10 days after election day) are checked and counted, and the rolls are checked for double voting. Results are published in the NZ Gazette and on electionresults.govt.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'

steps.text: Recounts and challenges: a candidate or party can apply for a recount within 3 working days of the official results; an election petition to the High Court must be filed within 28 days.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Forming a government: every electorate winner gets a seat; the rest are filled from party lists in proportion to the party vote. Under MMP one party rarely wins alone, so parties negotiate a coalition or support ('confidence and supply') deal. There is no deadline for this. The outgoing government stays on as a caretaker, avoiding major decisions, until a new one is sworn in.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What happens after an election?' (Government formation); RNZ The House, 2026

steps.text: The writ is returned by 3 December 2026 with the names of elected MPs; the new Parliament's three-year term runs from that day. Parliament must meet within 6 weeks of that date (Constitution Act 1986 s 19), so by 14 January 2027 even if coalition talks are still going. The first sitting day MPs are sworn in and elect a Speaker (Commission Opening); the next day the Governor-General gives the Speech from the Throne (State Opening).
steps.source: RNZ The House (Clerk of the House David Wilson), 2026; Constitution Act 1986 ss 17 and 19 (raw/howtovote/constitution-act-1986.pdf); vote.nz key dates

notes: Why specials lean a certain way is analysis, not Commission fact: 1News (3 Nov 2023) wrote that special votes 'have historically tended to skew left'. The guide reports the shifts, not the reasons.

In 2023 the official count took three weeks; the Chief Electoral Officer told MPs in September 2025 the 2025 law change would not make the 20-day official result faster, because people enrolling between Writ Day and the 13-day close still cast special votes (RNZ).
Voting papers are kept sealed for six months in case of a legal challenge, then destroyed (vote.nz).

Parliament's and DPMC's own post-election pages (election-2026-timeline, Cabinet Office circular CO (26) 5) could not be fetched (bot protection), so government-formation steps are sourced to vote.nz, RNZ's The House and the Constitution Act.

sections.title: 9. Check before you share: official sources and where to report
who_its_for: people who see election claims on social media

steps.text: The Electoral Commission's campaign, launched 29 July 2026, asks people to 'take a moment' before sharing information about enrolling and voting: 'slow down and check the information you see or hear. If you see something that doesn't look right on your social media feed, don't share it.' Waatea News reported it under the headline 'Think Before You Share'.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release, 29 Jul 2026; vote.nz 'Free and fair elections'; Waatea News, 30 Jul 2026

steps.text: Official sources for when, where and how to vote: vote.nz and 0800 36 76 56. For results: electionresults.govt.nz. The Commission's 'Facts about New Zealand elections' page answers common myths (no ID needed, no voting machines, hand counts, how specials work).
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Don't share misinformation even to correct it; post the correct information instead. Check that a claim really comes from a candidate's or party's real account or website. Election ads must carry a promoter statement (name and address); unpaid posts must show it on the account's About or Profile page.
steps.source: elections.nz 'Social media', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Where to report: misleading information about when, where or how to vote, or an ad with no promoter statement, to the Electoral Commission (elections.nz/contact, enquiries@elections.govt.nz, 0800 36 76 56). Paid or boosted social media ads: Advertising Standards Authority (asa.co.nz). TV and radio: Broadcasting Standards Authority. News content: the publisher, then the Media Council. Posts that break platform rules: report to the platform. The Commission refers suspected offences to Police; it does not regulate the content of political ads.
steps.source: elections.nz 'Advice and complaints' and 'Social media', retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: The Commission's own name for the campaign is not stated beyond the release title 'Take a moment before you share information'; 'Think before you share' is the media's phrasing (Waatea News). Not verified as an official slogan.
The Commission has referred several 2026 election advertising matters to Police (releases 16 and 23 Oct 2026); it names the rule breached, not the content.

could_not_verify: Official slogan of the Commission's misinformation campaign (release title is 'Take a moment before you share information'; 'Think before you share' is Waatea News' headline).

Access 2026 'Quick guide to accessible voting services' PDF and the NZSL resources page: blocked by bot protection; summarised from the Access 2026 web page, Easy Read page and the telephone dictation page.

Parliament.nz 'Election 2026 timeline' and DPMC Cabinet Office circular CO (26) 5 on post-election procedures: blocked; government-formation timing sourced instead to vote.nz, RNZ's The House and the Constitution Act 1986.

Date of the Electoral Amendment Act's third reading: Ministry of Justice says 16 December 2025; a web-search summary of RNZ gave 17 December. We use the Ministry's date. Royal assent 19 December 2025 and commencement 20 December 2025 are consistent across the Ministry, the consolidated Act and Wikipedia.

Whether the enrolment 'hub drop-off' is accepted right up to midnight 25 October: the Commission says forms can be dropped at hubs 'by 25 October'; hub hours vary (check vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/enrolment-in-your-community).
Licence for the Commission's voting-place data: none found; treated as not reusable (see voting_places).
electionresults.govt.nz itself could not be loaded from this environment (bot protection); the address is the one the Commission's key dates page links to for results.
howtovote.raw_sources_folder: raw/howtovote/ (HTML of each Commission page as fetched 23 Oct 2026, text extracts in raw/howtovote/txt/, the consolidated Electoral Act 1993 as at 1 Jan 2026 and Constitution Act 1986 PDFs from legislation.govt.nz, and the Commission's 'Rules once voting starts' PDF)

quiz2.about: Party positions on 30 statements, coded independently by two coders from published sources (manifesto first, then votes, questionnaire answers, dated statements, coalition actions) and reconciled by a third reviewer. Evidence, URL, tier and confidence are published for every cell. See guide/quiz-method.md and raw/quiz2/RECONCILIATION.md.

T.label: Te Tiriti and biculturalism
T.pole_b: one law for all, uniform treatment

D.label: Democracy and power
D.pole_a: direct democracy, limits on money, local autonomy

evidence_tiers.1: party's 2026 manifesto / policy document / policy page
evidence_tiers.2: recorded party vote in the 54th Parliament on legislation enacting or repealing the proposal
evidence_tiers.3: party's own written answer to a third-party questionnaire (Greenpeace, NZCTU, Grey Power, KPMG tracker)
evidence_tiers.4: dated statement by the leader or portfolio spokesperson
evidence_tiers.5: coalition agreement commitment or government action attributable to the party (flagged)

statements.text: The government should take active steps to reduce the gap between high and low incomes, even if that means higher taxes for some people.

national.evidence: Coder A: National's 2026 'no new taxes' pledge (23 Aug 2026) rules out any new tax including wealth or capital taxes; Fiscal Plan commits to reducing Crown spending toward 30% of GDP (9 Aug 2026). Willis: 'We will not introduce a capital gains tax' (28 Oct 2025). No redistribution-through-tax commitment anywhere in 2026 material. Coder B: No 2026 text on narrowing the income gap; National's fiscal plan rules out 'new taxes' and attacks Labour/Greens/TPM 'nine new taxes' as punishing 'Kiwis who do the right thing and save and invest' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026). Inference from explicit general principle (no higher taxes) -> disagree; recorded as inference. Reconciler: Both coders derive the value from the same 'no new taxes' pledge; neither found any 2026 text on narrowing the income gap. That is the permitted inference from an explicit general principle, which section 4.1(3) caps at +/-1 with low confidence. A's -2 (high) is reduced accordingly.

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 platform introduces a 28% CGT on investment and commercial property (announced 28 Oct 2025, applies from 1 Jul 2027), ring-fenced to fund free GP visits and other health spending; it also commits to higher minimum wages and restoring pay equity. Redistribution is a theme but the tax is narrow and the family home, farms, shares and business assets are exempt, so support is qualified.

green.evidence: 2026 tax policy 'A tax system for all of us' (21 Jun 2026): 2.5% wealth tax on net assets over $10m, capital acquisitions tax on large gifts/inheritances, 45% rate above $160,000, higher corporate taxes, funding a $10,000 tax-free threshold and income tax cuts for 96% of earners. Grey Power response: tax policy 'will redistribute wealth'.

act.evidence: Coder A: ACT 2026 Fiscal Plan cuts non-frontline spending to 2017 levels per person and 'pays down debt faster'; ACT 'strongly opposes any new tax, because once they're in, they always grow' (Free Press, 17 Aug 2026); Seymour on Labour's CGT: 'Another tax is not the solution to our problems' (28 Oct 2025). Coder B: Fiscal Plan 2026 cuts spending to 2017 per-person levels and rules out new taxes; Seymour (CA ANZ forum, 21 Sep 2026): the problem is public-sector productivity, 'not too little revenue'; ACT campaigns against wealth/asset taxes as 'envy taxes'. Emphasised rejection of higher taxes for redistribution.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First would cut the company tax rate to 20% for firms under $30m turnover (24 Sep 2026) and increase the In-Work Tax Credit by $70/week funded from existing spending; Peters called Labour's CGT 'an absolute mess of an announcement' (28 Oct 2025). Supports some redistribution (WFF, minimum wage) but opposes higher taxes to pay for it. Coder B: Peters attacks 'neoliberal' asset sales and wants a state bank, higher minimum wage with inflation and a $70 In-Work Tax Credit rise, but also calls TOP's/Greens' wealth taxes 'communism' (13 Sep 2026) and proposes a 20% SME tax rate. Both sides emphasised -> argued neutral. Reconciler: A (-1) and B (0) document the same two facts: NZ First proposes redistribution (In-Work Tax Credit rise, minimum-wage indexation, state bank) and simultaneously rejects higher taxes (SME tax cut; wealth taxes called 'communism', 13 Sep 2026). The statement is a trade-off and the party emphasises both sides without choosing: EUvox argued-neutral case 2. Consistent with its E2 and E7 codings.

te-pati-maori.evidence: 'A Kiwi Tax Plan' (Aug 2026): first $30,000 tax-free, six bands with a 48% top rate above $300,000, tiered wealth tax from 1.5% on net wealth over $2m, 5% stamp duty; explicitly aimed at shifting the tax burden from low earners to the wealthy.

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset: 1.75% land value tax and three income tax rates (28/34/39%) funding a universal Citizens' Income of up to $370/week and Child Support Incomes; designed to lift low incomes while taxing land wealth, though the party frames it as a 'reset' rather than a redistributive tax rise.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies address 'economic inequality' and reducing inequality through employment law and transition support; no tax policy stated. Qualified, low. Reconciler: Explicit commitment to reduce economic inequality through employment law and transition support; no tax measure. Partial: +1 low.

alliance.evidence: Alliance Tax Justice policy (Sep 2026): first $20,000 tax-free, upper rates of 34/39/47%, a 2.5% annual wealth tax on net wealth over $2m, a 33% CGT and a financial transactions levy, explicitly to shift tax from wages onto wealth; party describes itself as democratic socialist.

conservative.evidence: Coder A: Conservative economy policy: cut personal and company tax, align the company rate with the top personal rate, lower GST to 12.5%, and a 2025 release calls for a flat tax; 'We support lower taxes, responsible spending' (2026 site). Coder B: Finance policy: 'press for a flat tax rate for individuals and for companies'; principles: New Zealanders 'free to enjoy the fruits of their labour to the greatest possible extent'. Explicit principle against redistributive taxation; qualified. Reconciler: Flat tax and lower taxes are explicit and emphasised, but the party says nothing about the income gap itself; the value is an inference from an explicit tax principle, so -1 under section 4.1(3). Confidence medium because the flat-tax commitment is a direct rejection of progressive taxation.

womens-rights.evidence: 'Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes'; CPAG-style Working for Families reform for 'the poorest families'. No tax measure; qualified, low. Reconciler: Explicit: raise minimum wages and benefits 'so that all people have living incomes' and target Working for Families at the poorest. Direction explicit, tax side unaddressed: +1 low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Universal Whānau Allowance, debt amnesty, 25% mana whenua equity in regional infrastructure, living-wage trade academy - redistribution without a stated tax measure; qualified, low. Reconciler: Universal Whānau Allowance, debt amnesty and mana whenua equity stakes are explicit redistribution; no tax measure: +1 low.

statements.explainer: Income inequality is usually measured by comparing the highest-earning households with the lowest. Reducing the gap can be done through higher taxes on high incomes, bigger transfers like benefits and tax credits, or higher minimum pay. The trade-off is that some people keep less of what they earn so that others receive more. Agree if you think narrowing the gap is worth that; disagree if you think people should keep more of their own income even if the gap stays wide.

statements.text: Lower taxes do more good for New Zealand than more government spending, even if it means fewer public services.

national.evidence: Coder A: National: 'keep taxes low', no new taxes, reduce Crown expenditure toward 30% of GDP, return to surplus by 2028/29 (Aug 2026); but also funds Pharmac, school lunches, paid parental leave extensions, so 'fewer public services' is not embraced. Supports the direction with qualifications. Coder B: Fiscal Plan (Oct 2026): 'not impose new taxes', 'show ongoing restraint so that overall government expenditure comes down towards 30% of GDP', 'right-sizing government'; but also pledges to 'continue investing in health, schools, law and order' - so a qualified preference for lower tax/smaller state.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour would raise a CGT to fund Medicard free GP visits, free prescriptions and other services; targets core Crown spending and revenue of about 33% of GDP (higher than National's 30%) and would reverse planned public service cuts (Fiscal Plan). Prefers service spending over tax cuts. Coder B: Fiscal Strategy 2026: 'balance the books without shrinking the economy'; funds Medicard, free prescriptions and public-service restoration partly through a new CGT; attacks National's tax cuts 'to those at the top'. Prefers services over tax cuts, qualified.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens' 2026 manifesto: 'Fund public services adequately', Green Budget 2025 expands health, education, income support funded by wealth and corporate taxes; tax policy raises net revenue from the super-rich to pay for services. Coder B: Greens fund free ECE, dental, fees-free and public housing by taxing 'the super-rich and large corporates'; manifesto: 'fund public services adequately'; Green Budget 2025 raises revenue and borrowing rather than cutting.

act.evidence: Fiscal Plan 2026: 'reducing spending to 2017 levels adjusted for wages, inflation and population', cut new spending from $2.4b to $2b, consolidate 43 departments to 19; balancethebooks.nz: 'ACT will pay down debt faster'; tax cuts funded from smaller government.

nz-first.evidence: NZ First proposes both tax cuts (20% company rate for SMEs) and large new spending (a $100bn Future Fund for infrastructure, $5,000-a-year Kiwi Kids Grant, higher WFF, universal Super protected). Argued neutral: both sides emphasised, no stated preference for lower taxes over services. Reconciler: Tax cuts (20% SME rate) and very large new spending ($100bn Future Fund, Kiwi Kids Grant) proposed together with no stated preference: both sides emphasised, argued neutral. Consistent with E1 and E7.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Kiwi Tax Plan raises revenue from wealth and high incomes to fund doubled baseline benefits, a $4.5bn Oranga Whenua Oranga Tangata Fund, Māori health/education/justice authorities; the policy tool prioritises public spending over tax cuts.

opportunity.evidence: Coder A: Opportunity's Tax Reset is revenue-shifting (land value tax to fund a Citizens' Income) and it proposes a $60bn Infrastructure Fund, a 10-year health plan with 'predictable increases to baselines' and restored polytechnic funding (Grey Power response, 2026). Does not favour lower taxes at the expense of services. Coder B: Tax Reset shifts tax onto land to fund a universal income and keeps revenue; infrastructure policy to borrow for $60b of investment; 10-year health plan lifting funding to 9% of GDP. Opposes smaller-state framing; qualified.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: 'Smaller, leaner central government', 'Ending Bureaucratic Waste', shrink central ministries; no tax-cut pledge. Qualified, low. Reconciler: 'Smaller, leaner central government', shrink ministries and 'end bureaucratic waste' is an explicit general principle whose scope plainly covers preferring a smaller state to more services: +1 low.

alliance.evidence: Alliance: free GP, dental, optical and audiology care, universal benefits, free public transport, 52 weeks paid parental leave, funded by wealth, capital gains and higher income taxes (Tax Justice policy, Sep 2026).

conservative.evidence: Coder A: 'We support lower taxes, responsible spending and fewer unnecessary regulations'; cut personal, company tax and GST; health 'the key issue is whether patients are treated in time, not how much is spent' (2026 site). Coder B: Small Government page: 'over-governed, over-regulated, and over-taxed'; 'Government spending and borrowing... must be slashed'; cut personal and company tax, GST to 12.5%; 'shrink government so that it focuses on its core business'.

statements.explainer: Governments can lower taxes, which leaves people with more money to spend as they choose, or keep taxes up and fund more public services (health, schools, transport, welfare). You cannot have the maximum of both. Agree if you think people spending their own money does more good; disagree if you think pooled spending on services does more good.

statements.text: Gains people make from rising property and asset values should be taxed in the same way as income from work.

national.evidence: Coder A: Nicola Willis, 28 Oct 2025: National 'will not introduce a capital gains tax', calling Labour's plan 'an attack on investment and savings'; Luxon: 'a tax on every single business'. 2026 'no new taxes' pledge (23 Aug 2026) rules out any new tax. Coder B: 'No new taxes, including no capital gains tax' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026); Luxon 21 Jun 2026: 'not smashing ambition with a Capital Gains Tax'; 'New Zealand's lack of a capital gains tax is a real competitive advantage' (23 Aug 2026).

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 CGT: a flat 28% on gains from residential investment and commercial property only, excluding the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets and inheritances (announced 28 Oct 2025). Supports taxing some asset gains, but at a flat rate on a narrow base rather than 'in the same way as income from work'.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens' 2026 tax policy taxes wealth directly (2.5% on net assets over $10m), taxes large gifts and inheritances, and restores a 10-year bright-line test and removes interest deductibility; Swarbrick called Labour's property-only CGT 'watered down' and 'far short' (28 Oct 2025). Clear, emphasised support for taxing asset wealth and gains. Coder B: Standing economic policy: 'expanding the progressive tax system to equitably tax wealth and all forms of income, such as through capital gains, land, wealth, and inheritance taxes'; 2026 wealth tax and capital acquisitions tax; criticised Labour's CGT as too limited.

act.evidence: Coder A: Seymour on Labour's CGT: 'Another tax is not the solution to our problems' (28 Oct 2025); ACT policies cut tax on capital (no tax on KiwiSaver earnings; landlords may offset rental losses, 'abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes'). Coder B: KPMG 2026 tracker records ACT: 'No capital gains tax', 'No wealth tax/inheritance tax', tax exemption for crypto gains held over a year; ACT releases attack Labour's 'capital gains caucus' (2026). Consistent long-standing opposition.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: Peters called Labour's CGT 'an absolute mess of an announcement' (28 Oct 2025); NZ First vetoed a CGT in 2019 ('would not budge') and has never supported a broad capital gains tax. No 2026 policy to tax capital gains. Coder B: KPMG 2026 tracker: NZ First 'Not stated' on CGT and 'Not stated, has previously opposed such taxes' on wealth tax; Peters 13 Sep 2026 derides TOP's land tax and Green asset taxes. Inference from explicit rejection of wealth/land taxes; low. Reconciler: Peters' derision of Labour's CGT (Oct 2025) and of wealth/land taxes (Sep 2026) is explicit opposition, but there is no 2026 policy document and KPMG's tracker records 'not stated'. -2 requires an emphasised, unconditional position; -1 fits.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Kiwi Tax Plan: wealth tax on net assets, 2% vacant house tax, land-banking tax, 5% stamp duty, repeal landlord interest deductibility; taxes asset holdings rather than realised gains like income - partial match. Reconciler: The Kiwi Tax Plan (Aug 2026) taxes net wealth, vacant houses, land-banking and residential sales (stamp duty) but contains no capital gains tax: the archived plan never mentions capital gains. The statement is about taxing gains like income; taxing asset holdings is a partial match, so +1 (B's reading).

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset: 1.75% annual land value tax (0.5% rural) because 'work is heavily taxed while untaxed capital gains on housing enrich property owners'. Taxes land wealth annually rather than realised gains as income, so partial support.

alliance.evidence: Alliance Tax Justice policy: 33% capital gains tax on realised gains (excluding the family home) covering investment property, shares and business assets, plus a 2.5% wealth tax over $2m (Sep 2026).

statements.explainer: Income from a job is taxed as it is earned. Gains made when a house, shares or a business rise in value are, with some exceptions, not taxed in New Zealand. Taxing those gains like wages would raise revenue and treat different kinds of income the same, but would also reduce returns for people who own assets, including retirement savings and family homes if they were included. Agree if you think all income should be treated alike; disagree if you think gains on assets should be treated differently from wages.

statements.text: Services like electricity, housing and transport are delivered better by private businesses competing than by government ownership.

national.evidence: Luxon has called for a 'mature conversation' about selling assets the Crown has no reason to hold and asset recycling after the 2026 election (Nov 2025; reported Aug 2026); National's Electrify NZ keeps generation market-based with consistent transmission pricing for public and private players, and it uses PPPs/private finance in infrastructure. No sales this term; support for private delivery is qualified.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour: NZ Future Fund built on existing government assets 'keeping our assets in Kiwi hands' (10 Nov 2025); Hipkins says Labour is not considering asset sales beyond day-to-day housing churn and that under National-ACT 'there won't be anything left to sell'. Opposes privatisation but does not propose renationalisation. Coder B: NZ Future Fund: seeded state assets 'cannot be sold and will remain in public ownership for generations'; retain NZ ownership of Kiwibank; Hipkins on asset sales: 'there won't be anything left to sell'. Opposes privatisation; not an explicit claim that state delivery is better.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens would create Kiwipower, a publicly owned electricity firming company (20 Jul 2026), bring 120 supermarket stores into public ownership, build thousands of Kāinga Ora homes and ensure 'public services (and state-owned enterprises) remain in public hands' (manifesto 2026, public services). Coder B: Kiwipower publicly owned electricity firm ('Public ownership'), KiwiMart public supermarket, 'tens of thousands of new public homes', replace Public Transport Operating Model so services are 'provided publicly instead of for profit'; public services and SOEs to 'remain in public hands'.

act.evidence: Coder A: Seymour, 24 Jan 2025: government is 'hopeless at owning things', pushed privatisation and selling Landcorp; ACT proposes public-private partnerships for cancer centres and opposes forced break-ups of gentailers (2026). Long-standing emphasised position. Coder B: Electricity policy 2026: 'Open transmission to private investment'; opposes forced break-up of gentailers; cancer centres via public-private partnerships and private capital; charter schools to 10,000 places; Seymour urged a 'principle' on selling Air New Zealand (2025).

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: 'No government with New Zealand First will be selling our assets' (Peters, 17 May 2026); NZ First would buy BNZ back into NZ ownership, break up the gentailers and 'stop this economic privatisation madness' (State of the Nation, 22 Mar 2026). Coder B: 'Backing a New Zealand owned bank': buy back BNZ as a large state-owned bank; break up the gentailers; Peters condemns parties that 'sell our assets, privatise our country' and reports of Kiwibank/Air NZ sales (17 May 2026); 'no asset sales'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Coder A: TPM rejects privatisation and trading of water rights (Freshwater chapter 2026), proposes a $1bn Māori energy sovereignty fund and stronger regulator powers over power prices, and 'we want cheaper power and we want our people to own it'. Coder B: Freshwater policy: 'Reject privatisation and trading of water rights'; energy sovereignty plan with stronger Commerce Commission/Electricity Authority powers over prices; 2,000 papakāinga and half of new social housing for whānau Māori. Opposes privatisation; not a general ownership doctrine. Reconciler: Explicit rejection of privatising water rights and a Māori energy-ownership fund, but no general position on private versus public delivery across electricity, housing and transport. Equal evidence and tier; nearer-zero rule gives -1.

opportunity.evidence: Abundant Energy: ring-fence Crown gentailer dividends and restructure the market for competition; supports Kāinga Ora plus community providers; free public transport publicly funded. Both competition and public ownership emphasised -> argued neutral. Other coder: Opportunity would retain Crown stakes in the gentailers and use the money to fund 30GW of renewables, consolidate lines companies from 29 to fewer public/community entities, and expand Kāinga Ora and community housing; no privatisation proposed (Abundant Energy policy). Reconciler: Abundant Energy keeps Crown stakes in the gentailers and restructures the market for competition; housing policy backs both Kāinga Ora and community providers. Both sides stated by design: argued neutral (B, medium).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Fisheries policy: marine resources 'owned by the people of New Zealand... cannot become the private property of corporations'; housing policy uses 'a mixture of public and private housing model' and a hands-on Ministry of Housing. Favours public ownership of resources, mixed on services.

alliance.evidence: Public Ownership policy (Oct 2026): 're-integrate electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail under public ownership'; return ports, water, telecoms and Air NZ to full public ownership; 100% publicly owned transport system; state-house rebuilding.

conservative.evidence: Coder A: Mixed: health policy would 'buy private capacity where it is quicker and competitive'; natural resources policy proposes a Norway-style public-private resource JV but also state-bought oil tankers and new refineries. No general position on public v private delivery; argued neutral. Coder B: Mixed: 'the private sector prevailing over State control' and buying private hospital capacity, but also a state oil-tanker fleet, new state-backed refineries and a Norway-style public resource venture. Both sides -> argued neutral.

statements.text: Farmers and industry should pay for the greenhouse gases they emit, even if that raises food and fuel prices.

Labour will urgently review the ETS' to 'maintain a genuine price on emissions' but made no commitment to price agricultural emissions. Coder B: Manifesto 2026: 'Introduce a price on agricultural emissions'; reform ETS to remove free allocation and forestry offsetting; Greenpeace Q17 'We will bring agricultural emissions into the ETS'.

opportunity.evidence: Coder A: Climate Action policy: strengthen the ETS and add a mechanism for agricultural emissions; to Greenpeace it would 'explore a cap-and-trade market or novel levy structure' for methane rather than commit. Coder B: 'Strengthen the Emissions Trading Scheme and include agriculture' (policy.nz summary of climate policy); Greenpeace Q17: 'explore a cap-and-trade market or novel levy structure' for methane - supports direction without firm commitment.

Reconciler: 'End climate accords based on faulty science' and 'save our farmers from restrictive regulations' plainly cover emissions pricing on farmers, but the value is an inference from general principles, so reduced from -2 to -1 low under section 4.1(3).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Agriculture policy: withdraw from Paris, 'farm animals cannot release more carbon than they eat', 'we should celebrate carbon, not fear it'; opposes paying for Paris 'taxes'. Reconciler: Verified in the archived agriculture policy: exit Paris because it is 'far more expensive to stay and pay their taxes'; 'farm animals cannot release more carbon than they eat'; 'we should celebrate carbon, not fear it'. animal-justice.evidence: Coder A: AJP: 'cut emissions rapidly by shrinking animal agriculture' and include environmental externalities in economic measures; no explicit pricing mechanism. Coder B: Habitat policy: 'Redirect funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes and regulations'; 'internalising environmental and social costs' for polluters; no explicit emissions-pricing scheme. alliance.evidence: 'Replace the Emissions Trading Scheme with a carbon tax' with a transparent price; 'strict polluter-pays principle'; support farmers to 'reduce agricultural emissions'.

conservative.evidence: 'All taxes and restrictions on fossil fuels which are based on climate ideology should be scrapped'; scrap the ETS; end public funding of methane research.

statements.explainer: New Zealand puts a price on most greenhouse gas emissions through the Emissions Trading Scheme, but agricultural emissions, about half the national total, are not priced. Pricing them would give farmers a reason to cut emissions and would raise the cost of some food; pricing industry more would raise fuel and energy prices. Agree if you think emitters should pay even if prices rise; disagree if you think the cost to households and farms is too high.

statements.text: Big infrastructure, mining and energy projects should be able to go ahead faster, even if environmental checks are reduced.

national.evidence: Coder A: National passed the Fast-track Approvals Act (17 Dec 2024, along party lines) and in 2026 would issue a government policy statement ensuring mining and extraction can access the fast-track process; Greenpeace: National supports the Planning and Natural Environment Bills removing public participation. Coder B: Passed the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (3rd reading 17 Dec 2024); 2026 policy to add a mining/extraction policy statement under the Fast-track Act and to replace the RMA; 'say yes to growth more often'.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour voted against the Fast-track Approvals Bill (Dec 2024) and would 'fix the Fast-track Approvals Act so that environmental protections are not overridden, there is public participation' rather than repeal it (Greenpeace 2026). Coder B: Voted against the Fast-track Approvals Act (Dec 2024); Greenpeace Q23: 'Labour will fix the Fast-track Approvals Act so that environmental protections are not overridden' - retains a fast-track with safeguards, so qualified disagree.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens voted against Fast-track (2024), vowed to revoke fast-tracked projects, and oppose 'moves to reduce the ability for people to participate' (Greenpeace 2026). Coder B: Manifesto 2026: 'Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act and revoke consents for fast-track approvals for new coal, gold and seabed mining projects'; voted against the Act.

act.evidence: Voted for Fast-track Approvals Act 2024; 2026 mineral policy: 'Increase the flexibility around environmental regulations for mining', statutory compensation body for mineral investors, let routine farm work proceed without consent.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First's Shane Jones co-sponsored the Fast-track Approvals Act; to Greenpeace (2026) NZ First wants consenting 'faster, clearer and less bureaucratic', 'not necessarily a return to previous consenting systems'; mining zones and longer permits. Coder B: Grey Power response 2026 credits 'the Fast Track legislation which has allowed for faster approvals'; Greenpeace: supports planning 'faster, clearer and less bureaucratic'; sponsor of Fisheries Amendment Bill; voted for Fast-track Act.

Qualified disagree. Other coder: Opportunity to Greenpeace (2026): 'Yes' to restoring strong and enforceable environmental protections and public participation in all resource consenting legislation; repeal the Regulatory Standards Act. Reconciler: Greenpeace answer 'Yes' to restoring enforceable protections in consenting, but the Affordable Housing policy seeks faster consenting: qualified disagree (B).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Agriculture policy: apply the precautionary principle to new technology with full liability for businesses; independent Health-Environment Protection Agency. General principle against reduced checks; low confidence. Reconciler: Precautionary principle with full liability and an independent Health-Environment Protection Agency: explicit principles for more, not fewer, checks: -1 low.

Reconciler: Mandatory wildlife impact assessments in planning and road design is an explicit proposal for more environmental checks on projects: -1 low.

Reconciler: Mining bans, restoration bonds and a Conservation Minister veto all add checks, but the party has no statement on fast-track approvals themselves. Equal tier; nearer-zero rule: -1.

conservative.evidence: Agriculture policy: 'revisit the Planning and Natural Environment Bills to make them workable and protect property rights'; 'Fewer and less burdensome regulations'; 'Remove excessive red tape to speed up project approvals while maintaining environmental protections'. statements.explainer: Large projects need consents under environmental law, which can take years. Faster approval processes reduce delay and cost for things like roads, mines, wind farms and housing, but reduce the checks and public input that protect the environment and local communities. Agree if you think faster approvals are worth fewer checks; disagree if you think the checks should stay as they are.

statements.text: New Zealand should keep its international climate commitments even if other countries do less and it costs New Zealand economically.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Agriculture policy: withdraw from the Paris Agreement; 'That's nature, not climate change'; staying 'would cost more than leaving'.

statements.text: Extracting more minerals, oil and gas from New Zealand's land and waters is a good way to pay for public services.

opportunity.evidence: Coder A: Opportunity: permanently ban seabed mining; a reinstated offshore ban is 'probably unnecessary' but it 'would not oppose' one; strong presumption against mining on conservation land with small alluvial exceptions (Greenpeace 2026). Coder B: Permanently ban seabed mining; reverse LNG terminal; Greenpeace Q16: reinstating the offshore oil-and-gas ban 'probably unnecessary' but would not oppose it; mining the conservation estate 'short term'. animal-justice.evidence: Environmental policies: 'End government underwriting and tax incentives for fossil fuel exploration, particularly... offshore oil and gas exploration'; mining 'destroy[s] underground habitats'; restrict seabed mining. Other coder: AJP: protect and restore natural habitats, economy of 'sufficiency within planetary boundaries'. No explicit extraction statement; low-confidence inference. Reconciler: B's quotation verified in the archived policy: 'End government underwriting and tax incentives for fossil fuel exploration, particularly ... offshore oil and gas'; restrict seabed mining; mining 'destroys underground habitats'. alliance.evidence: Ban mining in national parks, conservation land and the Coromandel; 'transition away from dependence on fossil fuels'; electricity to be renewable and public.

conservative.evidence: Natural Resources: 'Actively encourage commercial oil and gas exploration', Norway-style joint venture, 'Hold the returns in a New Zealand Investment Fund... for future generations'; royalties shared with communities.

statements.explainer: New Zealand has coal, gold, oil and gas, and other minerals on land and offshore. Extracting more would bring royalties, jobs and export income that could fund public services; it also carries environmental risks and adds to emissions. Agree if you think more extraction is a good way to pay for services; disagree if you do not.

statements.text: New Zealand should let in fewer immigrants, even if some businesses cannot find the workers they need.

national.evidence: Coder A: National's 2026 policies expand and expedite migration (Active Investor Plus visa retention, expedited partner visas, vet bonding open to residents) and target growth; no proposal to reduce numbers. Coder B: Economic Plan 2026: 'Changed immigration settings to ensure New Zealand is attracting the skills we need'; Luxon called 118,800 net migration 'unsustainable' (2023) but 2026 policy emphasises attracting skilled migrants and investors. Addressed only vaguely -> argued neutral. Reconciler: National's 2026 measures target investors and skilled migrants and say nothing about overall numbers; Luxon's 2023 'unsustainable' remark cuts the other way. Addressed without a direction on numbers: argued neutral. Equal tier and confidence; nearer-zero rule.

Argued neutral. Other coder: Labour immigration policy (2026): a Government Policy Statement setting immigration to reflect workforce needs, extend permanent residence eligibility to four years, let migrants move between accredited employers, Pacific visa waivers. Manages rather than cuts migration. Reconciler: Labour's Sep 2026 policy plans immigration 'around what the workforce, housing and infrastructure can support' (verified on labour.org.nz/immigration) with no target for fewer or more. Argued neutral (B, medium).

Reconciler: Every Green proposal expands migration pathways, but the manifesto contains no statement on overall numbers; -2 requires an emphasised unconditional position. -1 medium.
