Migrants bring skills and help businesses grow', with a temporary $6/day visa surcharge for infrastructure; physical-presence test for residents and expanded deportation. Pro-immigration with conditions -> qualified disagree.

nz-first.evidence: Immigration reform (11 Sep 2026): referendum on a legislated cap of 20,000 resident visas a year, remove student work rights, temporary refugee status; Peters condemns 'mass immigration' (22 Mar 2026).

opportunity.evidence: Breakthrough Economy: 'a population policy for stable long-term immigration' linked to infrastructure, while attracting 'the best and brightest globally'. Both sides stated, no direction on numbers; argued neutral.

alliance.evidence: Foreign policy: 'review and reduce unnecessary barriers to migration from neighbouring Pacific Island countries'; no overall numbers position. Qualified disagree, low. Reconciler: 'Review and reduce unnecessary barriers to migration from neighbouring Pacific Island countries' moves toward more migrants for one region; partial: -1 low.

conservative.evidence: Immigration policy: skilled migrants only; 'net immigration should be capped based on a broad measure of social goods... If our social goods are not increasing, net immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers and their dependents should be zero'.

vision-nz.evidence: 'Pause mass immigration immediately to review visa policies and relieve pressure on local infrastructure and communities'; 10-year residency for citizenship; end dual citizenship for new applicants.

statements.explainer: Migration adds workers, skills and demand to the economy and also adds pressure on housing and infrastructure. Lower migration can ease that pressure and lift wages in some jobs but leave some businesses short of staff. Agree if you think New Zealand should admit fewer migrants even with staff shortages; disagree if you think current or higher levels are right.

statements.text: New migrants should wait several years before they can receive benefits and other public support.

national.evidence: Welfare policy (Oct 2026): extend the wait before new residents can access main benefits from 2 years to 5 years, 'in line with Australia and the UK'.

act.evidence: 'Deport serious offenders' policy page (2026): introduce a benefit stand-down for the first years of a residence visa; coalition partner in National's welfare settings.

nz-first.evidence: Immigration reform (11 Sep 2026): 'benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants', superannuation and social housing for citizens first, longer residency and citizenship eligibility.

alliance.evidence: Welfare policy abolishes 'unnecessary stand-down periods' and makes benefits a universal entitlement based on 'dignity' - scope plainly covers migrant stand-downs though migrants are not named; inference, low. Reconciler: Welfare policy abolishes 'unnecessary stand-down periods' and makes income support a universal entitlement based on dignity: an explicit principle whose scope plainly covers migrant stand-downs: -1 low.

statements.explainer: Most new residents can access some benefits and public support after two years; some supports have longer waits. A longer wait reduces costs to taxpayers and asks newcomers to contribute first; it also leaves some migrant families without a safety net if things go wrong. Agree if you think several years is a fair wait; disagree if you think newcomers should have access sooner.

statements.text: New Zealand should keep an independent foreign policy rather than tying itself more closely to traditional military allies, even if that means less protection.

national.evidence: Coder A: Defence Capability Plan (7 Apr 2025): $12bn over four years, defence spending to 2% of GDP, NZDF 'a force multiplier with Australia and interoperable with partners'; Collins: 'We are interested in being involved in pillar two' of AUKUS; Luxon (Jun 2026): capability 'to keep our people, and our partners, safe'. Coder B: Luxon conference speech 21 Jun 2026: 'Boosting defence spending and investing in the cutting-edge capability we need to protect our region'; Luxon wants NZ to be a 'force multiplier' for Australia and is scoping AUKUS Pillar 2. National still describes its foreign policy as independent, so qualified disagree.

labour.evidence: 'A Labour Government will not join AUKUS' pillar one or two (1 Dec 2024, restated 2026); 'restoring our independent foreign policy'. Also wants to 'strengthen and revitalise relationships with traditional partners', so qualified.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026 (Global affairs): 'Decouple military and security frameworks from the United States, including declining to participate in AUKUS and withdrawing from Five Eyes'; defence focused on climate and humanitarian response.

act.evidence: Mineral policy 2026 frames resource development as providing 'strategic resources to our allies'; ACT backed higher defence spending and AUKUS Pillar 2 scoping in government; no 2026 foreign-policy manifesto found. Qualified disagree, partly inferred. Reconciler: ACT's 2026 minerals policy frames development as providing 'strategic resources to our allies' (verified), and ACT campaigns for defence spending of 2% of GDP arguing New Zealand must pay to keep its Australian alliance credible (act.org.nz, 'God defend New Zealand'). Direction toward allies, no explicit alliance doctrine: -1 low.

nz-first.evidence: As Foreign Minister, Peters strengthened ties with the US, Australia and Pacific partners and kept AUKUS Pillar 2 under consideration ('a long way from a decision', 2024); 2026 speeches stress 'Western values' and defence experience. No explicit alliance policy; qualified disagree, low. Other coder: Peters: NZ's independent foreign policy 'does not, and never has, meant we are a non-aligned nation', AUKUS Pillar 2 exploration would be 'irresponsible not to' (2024); yet NZ First's 'sovereignty' pillar and opposition to foreign influence. Both sides; argued neutral. Reconciler: Peters as Foreign Minister said independence 'never meant non-aligned', pursued AUKUS Pillar 2 exploration and deepened US/Australia ties. A's counterweight ('sovereignty' rhetoric) concerns foreign influence and the UN, not military alliances, so it does not make an argued neutral. -1 low.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Military neutrality policy: declare NZ 'militarily neutral', review all alliances and withdraw from those that undermine neutrality, focus the Defence Force on the Pacific and disaster response.

alliance.evidence: 'independent, non-aligned, and peaceful nation'; 'We reject the idea that security is achieved through military alliances'; withdraw from inconsistent alliances, review foreign military and intelligence facilities.

conservative.evidence: 'Trade before War should be New Zealand's axiom. Taking a neutral stance rather than being dragged into war confrontations... should be a priority'; defence focused on support and reconstruction; but 'New Zealand must retain close' defence ties (text truncated). Qualified agree.

free-palestine.evidence: Founding principle 6: 'New Zealand commit to an independent foreign policy by withdrawing itself from any formal security alliances with the U.S. and by distancing our foreign policy from the orbit of Anglo-U.S. economic hegemony and military interventionism'.

statements.explainer: New Zealand is a close partner of Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom but has kept some distance, for example its nuclear-free policy, and is not a member of every alliance arrangement. Closer alignment might bring more protection and influence; independence keeps more freedom of action and avoids being drawn into others' conflicts. Agree if you prefer an independent foreign policy; disagree if you favour closer alignment with traditional allies.

statements.pole_a: direct democracy, limits on money, local autonomy
statements.text: Major national decisions should be put to the public in binding referendums rather than decided by Parliament, even if that slows things down.

national.evidence: Luxon rejected a referendum on the Treaty Principles Bill and said an election result, not a referendum, would be an acceptable mandate for asset sales (2025); in Aug 2026 he said he was open to a non-specified referendum on the electoral system. Generally prefers parliamentary decision; low confidence. Reconciler: Luxon refused a Treaty referendum ('it's a no from me', Jan 2025) and said an election, not a referendum, is the mandate for asset sales; he is 'open to' an electoral-system referendum (Reuters, Aug 2026, verified), the one domain where referendums are conventional. Pattern of preferring parliamentary decision, with a qualification: -1 low.

labour.evidence: Labour opposes NZ First's binding Māori seats referendum and said it opposed Luxon's proposed electoral-system referendum (Reuters, 5 Aug 2026); no direct-democracy policy. Low confidence. Reconciler: Verified: Labour opposed Luxon's proposed electoral-system referendum (Reuters, 5 Aug 2026) and NZ First's Māori-seats referendum (McAnulty, 12 Feb 2026: 'it is Māori that should decide'); no direct-democracy policy. -1 low.

green.evidence: Greens would entrench the Māori seats and reinstate councils' Māori wards against referendum override (2026); their only pro-referendum policy is local binding votes on casino licences. Opposes referendums on minority rights; no general direct-democracy policy. Other coder: Favours citizens' assemblies and community decision-making (local government chapter) and voted for referendum-based decisions only on local matters (casino licences); opposed referendums on Treaty principles and Māori seats. Topic addressed only indirectly -> argued neutral. Reconciler: The Greens oppose every national referendum proposed this term (Treaty principles, Māori seats; would entrench the seats against referendums) and have no direct-democracy policy; their only referendum proposal is local (casino licences). A pattern of explicit opposition to the proposed instruments: -1, low confidence because no general statement exists.

act.evidence: ACT campaigned for a binding referendum on its Treaty Principles Bill (2023-24) but opposed Luxon's electoral-system referendum idea (Aug 2026) and favours parliamentary supremacy in its Constitution Act proposal. Mixed; argued neutral. Other coder: ACT proposed a binding referendum on its Treaty Principles Bill (2023-25) and supported binding polls on Māori wards; no general binding-referendum policy in 2026 material. Qualified agree. Reconciler: ACT campaigned for a binding referendum on its Treaty Principles Bill (2023-25) and backed binding Māori-ward polls, but opposed Luxon's electoral-system referendum (Reuters, 5-6 Aug 2026, verified) and asserts parliamentary supremacy. Both sides on the record: argued neutral (A).

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First proposes binding referendums on the Māori seats (2026), on a 20,000 resident-visa cap, on conscience issues before they become law (Conscience Acts Referendums Bill, 2025) and local fluoridation referendums. Coder B: Binding referendum on the Māori seats (bill, Feb 2026); referendum on a 20,000 resident-visa cap (Sep 2026); member's bills requiring referendums before conscience issues become law and local referendums on fluoridation.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Waititi (13 Feb 2026): NZ First's binding Māori-seats referendum is 'a constitutional attack'; party rejected a referendum on Treaty principles, favouring Mātike Mai-led constitutional transformation. Opposes referendums deciding these questions; general stance inferred, low. Reconciler: Explicit opposition to referendums on the Māori seats ('beyond the reach of referendums') and Treaty principles, preferring a Matike Mai constitutional process. Specific to those questions, so -1 rather than -2; medium.

opportunity.evidence: Citizens' Voice: citizens' assemblies for major long-term decisions, with Government required to respond; 'This isn't about replacing elections or Parliament'; leader rejected a Treaty referendum (2023). Direct participation without binding referendums -> argued neutral. Reconciler: Citizens' Voice proposes citizens' assemblies for major decisions while stating 'this isn't about replacing elections or Parliament', and the leader rejected a Treaty referendum. Direct participation deliberately short of binding referendums: argued neutral (B, medium).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Direct Democracy: Swiss-style binding citizens' veto and citizen-initiated laws with low signature thresholds; 'the power of veto shifts entirely to you'; demand a binding referendum on direct democracy as a coalition condition.

alliance.evidence: Te Tiriti, Democracy and Constitutional policy (Sep 2026): constitutional review to examine 'Citizens' Initiatives, allowing citizens to propose legislative or policy changes', 'mechanisms for direct citizen participation', referendum on the monarchy.

statements.explainer: New Zealand is a representative democracy: Parliament makes most decisions, with occasional referendums. Binding referendums let voters decide big questions directly but take time and money, and can reduce a complex issue to yes or no. Agree if you want more major decisions put to a binding public vote; disagree if you think Parliament should decide.

statements.pole_a: direct democracy, limits on money, local autonomy
statements.text: Only individual voters on the electoral roll should be allowed to donate to political parties, even if parties then have less money to campaign.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour to Greenpeace (2026): 'Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations' without committing to voter-only donations; its Trust in Government policy adds third-party donation disclosure and a lobbying register. Addressed vaguely; argued neutral. Coder B: Greenpeace Q24 (voters-only donations): 'Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations' - no commitment; 2026 policy only extends disclosure to third-party campaigners. Vague -> argued neutral.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Reform electoral funding by limiting donations to registered voters, increasing public financing of campaigns and capping a donor's donations'; Greenpeace Q24 'Yes'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Coder A: TPM to Greenpeace (2026): 'Yes' to reforming electoral financing so only registered New Zealand voters can donate. Coder B: Greenpeace Q24 (only registered voters can donate): 'Yes'.

opportunity.evidence: Clean Up Politics: 'Ban donations from companies and trusts, so only registered New Zealand voters can donate', cap donations at $30,000 per donor per election, lower disclosure to $1,000.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies: 'Permit only New Zealand citizens or permanent residents registered to vote to make political donations, removing corporate/industry entity donations'; $30,000 cap per cycle; disclosure threshold $1,500. Other coder: AJP platform summary (Sep 2026): 'Lower donation limits and stronger disclosure rules', real-time lobbying reporting, cooling-off periods; does not propose voter-only donations. Reconciler: B's quotation verified in the archived People Policies pack: 'Permit only New Zealand citizens or permanent residents registered to vote to make political donations, removing corporate/industry entity donations', with a $1,500 disclosure threshold. Exactly the statement: +2.

alliance.evidence: 'strict transparency requirements for political donations... consider appropriate limits on political donations to prevent wealthy individuals, corporations, and other organisations from acquiring disproportionate political influence'; not an individuals-only rule. Qualified.

statements.explainer: Political parties can currently receive donations from individuals, companies, unions and other organisations, with disclosure rules above certain amounts. Limiting donations to enrolled voters would cut organisations' influence and reduce the money available to campaign. Agree if you think only individual voters should be able to donate; disagree if you think other donors should still be allowed.

statements.pole_a: direct democracy, limits on money, local autonomy
statements.text: Local councils should be free to make their own decisions, even if rates and rules then differ from place to place, rather than central government overriding them.

national.evidence: Coder A: National: instruct councils to keep rate rises between 2 and 4 percent with a regulator (26 Aug 2026), legislated compulsory referendums on Māori wards (2024), fast-track overriding council consenting. Coder B: Rates Capping Bill: councils' annual rate rises held to a 2-4% target range with an independent regulator (policy page, 2026); Government also required binding polls on Māori wards (2024).

labour.evidence: Labour supports the rates cap bill to select committee and is 'open to the idea of a rates cap in principle' (26 Aug 2026) while Hipkins earlier said capping rates would make infrastructure 'worse not better' (Jul 2025) and told the government to 'butt out' of council Māori ward decisions (2024). Mixed; argued neutral. Other coder: Voted against the 2024 law overriding council decisions on Māori wards by forcing binding polls (Hipkins: coalition 'embarrassing' NZ). No stated 2026 position on the rates cap found in sources checked; +1 inferred from that vote only, flagged. Reconciler: Labour is 'open to the idea of a rates cap in principle' (Aug 2026, centralising) after Hipkins called caps counter-productive (Jul 2025), and opposed the Māori-ward override (devolving). B's +1 rests on the single 2024 vote. Documented both-ways record: argued neutral (A).

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Reject the proposed rates cap and enable a range of new funding and financing tools'; 'empower councils by devolving further responsibilities'; reinstate councils' ability to keep Māori wards.

act.evidence: ACT: remove voting rights from unelected council appointees by law, require councils to compensate landowners for overlays, a Local Tourism Dividend instead of allowing councils new taxes, supports the rates cap as a coalition partner. Reconciler: Two-point disagreement. ACT's programme constrains councils at every turn: rates cap, binding Māori-ward polls, removing votes from unelected appointees by statute, mandated compensation rules, and opposition to councils' own bed tax. B's devolving item (a Local Tourism Dividend) is a funding transfer, not autonomy. A's evidence is directly on point: -2, medium.

nz-first.evidence: NZ First would return fluoridation decisions to local referendums and give regions 50% of mining royalties, yet legislates to disestablish Auckland's Independent Māori Statutory Board and backed compulsory Māori ward polls and the rates cap. Both directions; argued neutral.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Coder A: TPM opposed the 2024 law overriding councils' Māori ward decisions but would itself require Māori wards in every council and return council land to mana whenua. Mixed on council autonomy; argued neutral. Coder B: Would require Māori wards and mana whenua representation 'in all councils' (central mandate) while giving hapū and iwi the same disaster resources as councils and opposing coalition overrides. Mixed -> argued neutral.

opportunity.evidence: Coder A: Opportunity: give councils more tools (congestion charges, bed levies, value capture), 'ending unfunded mandates by central government', support LGNZ's ratepayer assistance scheme (Grey Power response 2026). Coder B: Intergenerational Infrastructure: 'Arbitrary, central government-imposed rate[s caps]' criticised; expand council funding tools and GST share; but an independent regulator would hold councils to asset-management standards. Qualified agree.

nz-loyal.evidence: 'Decentralise government and return power to the people' (website via RNZ, Oct 2026) - general principle covering council autonomy; inference, low.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Direct Democracy policy: decentralise under a 'subsidiarity' principle, let regions keep part of the GST and tax raised locally, 'no top-down political majority can ever dictate to your community'.

alliance.evidence: Coder A: What we stand for: 'A thriving national democracy requires healthy local democracy. Those who know best what communities need are those that live in them. Local communities should own and control services such as water, waste disposal, and public transport.' Coder B: Constitutional review to consider 'the role of local government'; end requirement for councils to put water into arms-length entities; repeal procurement rules forcing councils into corporatised public transport. Qualified agree.

conservative.evidence: Principles: 'Decision-making should be as local as possible... localism'; 'Local decision making'; mayors may become full-time council CEOs; ministers to appoint and sack senior officials. Qualified agree. Reconciler: Verified principle: 'Decision-making should be as local as possible through a principle known as localism ... higher levels of government should serve to empower and support lower levels of authority, rather than control or replace them'. Explicit: +1 medium.

statements.explainer: Councils make decisions about local services, planning and rates, but central government can set rules they must follow or override them. More local freedom means decisions fit local wishes but can differ from place to place; more central control brings consistency. Agree if you prefer local councils deciding; disagree if you prefer central government setting the rules.

scale.skip: No opinion / skip (excluded from the match)

scoring.party_scale: -2..+2 as coded; 0 = argued neutral (counts as a position); null = no position found (excluded, never shown as neutral)
scoring.agreement: a_ij = 1 - |u_i - p_ij| / 4   (city-block, in [0,1]) over S_j = statements the user answered and party j has a non-null position
scoring.raw_match: raw_j = sum_{i in S_j} w_i * a_ij / sum_{i in S_j} w_i

shrinkage.formula: match_j = (sum_{i in S_j} w_i * a_ij + k * 0.5) / (sum_{i in S_j} w_i + k)
shrinkage.note: shrinks toward the uninformative value 0.5 by k phantom neutral statements

coverage_rule.default_ranking_if: |S_j| >= max(10, 0.5 * M), where M = number of statements the user answered
coverage_rule.otherwise: listed separately with the badge 'based on only N of your M answers' and the shrunk score
coverage_rule.party_level_badge: parties with fewer than 15 of 30 coded positions carry a 'limited information' badge and are excluded from the default ranking

scoring.dimension_agreement: A_jd = sum_{i in d and S_j} w_i a_ij / sum_{i in d and S_j} w_i, reported as agreement on N of the dimension's statements

dimension_map.formula: x_d = mean_i(s_i * v_i) / 2 in [-1, +1], over the dimension's statements with a value; s_i = polarity_sign (+1 for '+A' items, -1 for '+B' items); v_i = user answer or party position
dimension_map.meaning: +1 = pole A, -1 = pole B; agreeing with a '+B' statement moves toward pole B
dimension_map.status: secondary illustration; the ranking uses all statements, never the map

scoring.uncertainty_band: recompute match_j (a) with every low-confidence party cell set to null and (b) with every +/-1 party cell moved one step toward and away from the user; show min-max as a thin band; show the count of low-confidence cells
display: ties within 2 points shown as ties
'based on N of your M answers' on every party
unweighted result beside the weighted one
statement order randomised per session, no topic headers while answering
party positions revealed only after all answers
unit_tests: skipped, no-opinion and null cells excluded

compass.about: A general political-values test ("compass"): 36 items from openly licensed or public survey instruments, scored onto an economic left-right axis, a GAL-TAN social axis and a secondary populism axis. Items are deliberately NOT about New Zealand election issues (see data/guide/quiz.json for that); parties are placed on the same axes from published expert data and from our own coding of their documents (data/guide/compass-parties.json).

economic.label: Economic left-right
economic.left_pole: Left: state intervention, redistribution, public ownership
economic.right_pole: Right: markets, limited government, fiscal restraint
economic.basis: Hooghe, Marks & Wilson (2002) economic left-right; CHES "lrecon"; Global Party Survey V4.

social.label: Social: libertarian/green-alternative (GAL) to traditional/authoritarian/nationalist (TAN)
social.left_pole: GAL / libertarian: personal freedom, pluralism, openness
social.right_pole: TAN / authoritarian: order, tradition, national culture
social.basis: Hooghe, Marks & Wilson (2002) GAL-TAN; Kitschelt (1994) libertarian-authoritarian; CHES "galtan"; Global Party Survey V6.

populism.label: Populist / anti-establishment attitudes
populism.left_pole: Pluralist: trusts representative institutions, compromise, minority rights
populism.right_pole: Populist: people vs. elite, popular sovereignty, anti-politician
populism.basis: Mudde (2004); Akkerman, Mudde & Zaslove (2014); CSES Module 5 "Democracy Divided?" elite battery; Global Party Survey V8.

compass.direction_key: +1 = agreeing (or feeling positive) moves the respondent toward the right / TAN-authoritarian / populist pole; -1 = reverse-keyed item.

response_values.likert5: -2 strongly disagree, -1 disagree, 0 neither, +1 agree, +2 strongly agree; a skipped item is null
response_values.feeling5: -2 very negative, -1 negative, 0 neutral, +1 positive, +2 very positive; a skipped item is null

scoring.keyed_score: keyed_i = direction_i * response_i   (so +2 always means the right / TAN-authoritarian / populist pole)
scoring.axis_score: axis = 5 * mean(keyed_i over answered items on that axis), giving -10 (left / GAL-libertarian / pluralist) .. +10 (right / TAN-authoritarian / populist)
scoring.min_items_rule: If fewer than min_items on an axis were answered, do not show a point on that axis; show "not enough answers" instead.

uncertainty.method: half-width = max(1.0, 1.96 * 5 * sd(keyed_i) / sqrt(n))  where sd is the sample standard deviation of the keyed item scores on that axis and n the number answered. The floor of 1.0 reflects that even a complete, perfectly consistent set of 5-point answers cannot locate a person more finely than about one unit on a 20-unit axis.
uncertainty.display: Show the point with an error bar (or shaded band) of +/- half-width, and the text "based on n of N items". With all items answered and sd = 0 the band is +/-1.0.

scoring.subscales: Each item carries a "subscale" tag (SECS economic, SECS social, VSA authoritarianism, CSES populism, WVS economic values, CSES out-group, ESS, NZES). A subscale score is 5 * mean(keyed_i) over the answered items with that tag; show it only when at least half of the subscale's items were answered. SECS subscale scores can also be shown on Everett's original 0-100 metric: secs_0_100 = 50 + 12.5 * mean(keyed_i) (equivalent to mapping -2..+2 onto 25..75; a fully "very positive" conservative answer set scores 75, not 100, because the 5-point version compresses the thermometer).
scoring.acquiescence: Within each axis roughly half the items are reverse-keyed (economic 6/6, social 10 TAN-keyed / 6 GAL-keyed, populism 7/1). A respondent who agrees with everything therefore lands near 0 on the economic axis; on the populism axis the CSES battery is mostly protrait, so the app should treat a populism score as indicative only and show it as a secondary axis.
scoring.party_comparison: Parties are scored with the same formula from their coded answers (data/guide/compass-parties.json: coded.axes). Distance between a user and a party on the two main axes is the Euclidean distance in the -10..+10 plane, shown only for axes where both have enough items.

compass_parties.about: NZ party placements on the compass axes from (a) published expert/manifesto/voter-survey data, each kept on its original scale with a stated rescaling to -10..+10, and (b) our own coding of each party's answers to the 36 compass items from its 2026 policy documents, recorded votes and leader statements (null = no evidence, never guessed). Scores in coded.axes use the same formula as the user test (data/guide/compass.json scoring). See guide/compass-method.md.
compass_parties.axes_scale: -10..+10 on every axis; economic: left (-) to right (+); social: GAL/libertarian (-) to TAN/authoritarian (+); populism: pluralist (-) to populist (+). "general_left_right" values are voters' or experts' overall left-right placements and are NOT the economic axis.
compass_parties.coding_scale: -2 strongly disagree / very negative .. +2 strongly agree / very positive relative to the item text; confidence high | medium | low; null = no public evidence found.

not_retrieved.name: Manifesto Project (MARPOR / CMP) RILE scores for NZ manifestos
not_retrieved.reason: The Manifesto Project Main Dataset (MPDS2024a) and its API require a free registered account and API key; the download could not be completed from this research environment and no published table of NZ RILE scores for 2017-2023 was found. The dataset covers NZ parties (CMP ids 64110 Green, 64320 Labour, 64420 ACT, 64620 National, 64621 NZ First, 64901 Māori Party per the CSES Module 5 codebook). RILE = share of right-coded quasi-sentences minus share of left-coded ones (-100..+100).
not_retrieved.proposed_rescale: economic approximation: RILE / 10 (so -100..+100 -> -10..+10); note RILE mixes economic and social categories.

not_retrieved.reason: Vote Compass places parties on a two-dimensional (economic x social) chart inside the application, from party answers to 30 propositions calibrated by the Vox Pop Labs team with NZ political scientists; the party coordinates are shown to users but are not published as numbers in 1News articles or in a dataset. 1News articles on 10 Oct 2023 and 22 Oct 2026 publish electorate-level scores only.

econ_wvs_incomes.evidence: "Reward for achievement" is a stated party value; "No new taxes, including no capital gains tax".

econ_wvs_responsibility.evidence: "those who can work should work ... Our welfare system provides a safety net when people need it, but it must be fair and affordable"; "Personal responsibility" is a party value.

econ_wvs_competition.evidence: "Competitive enterprise" is a party value; "Strong competition is one of the most effective ways to reduce prices, increase innovation, lift productivity".

econ_cses_reduce_differences.evidence: "No new taxes, including no capital gains tax."

econ_nzes_privatisation.evidence: Carried out the 2011-14 mixed-ownership share floats despite a referendum against them (dated evidence; no 2026 asset-sales policy found).

econ_nzes_big_business.evidence: Says "supermarket competition is still too weak" yet "businesses create wealth, not governments".

econ_secs_limited_government.evidence: Luxon lists "Limited government" among National's founding values (June 2026).

econ_secs_welfare_benefits.evidence: Reduce Jobseeker payments after two years; random drug testing; five-year stand-down for new residents.

econ_secs_business.evidence: "businesses create wealth, not governments"; "Competitive enterprise" value.

electorates.name: Auckland Central
electorates.description: Auckland Central covers Auckland’s city centre, suburbs such as Ponsonby, Newton and Arch Hill, as well as the islands of the Hauraki Gulf. It is currently held by Green party co-leader Chlöe Swabrick, who won the electorate with a margin of 16,624 votes and has held the seat since 2020. National won the party vote in 2023 with 33%, followed by the Green Party on 24%. Barring one three year gap, the seat was held continuously by Labour from 1919-2008, but it has not regained it since.
description_fact_check: "margin of 16,624" (that figure is the winner’s vote total) — the official 2023 majority was 3,896 votes over Mahesh Muralidhar.

Pollster David Farrar says all three Green-held seats could be regarded as marginal.

electorates.name: Banks Peninsula
electorates.description: Banks Peninsula covers the area to the east and south of Christchurch, including Akaroa, Lyttleton, and southern Christchurch suburbs such as Oaklands, Woolston, and Kennedys Bush. It is held by National’s Vanessa Weenink, who narrowly won the electorate for the first time in 2023 with a margin of 17,860. National also won the party vote with 32% of the vote, followed by Labour at 27%. The electorate had the highest turnout of any electorate at the 2023 election.
description_fact_check: "margin of 17,860" (that figure is the winner’s vote total) — the official 2023 majority was 396 votes over Tracey McLellan.

electorates.name: Botany
electorates.description: Botany covers much of East Auckland, including the suburbs of East Tamaki, Flat Bush, Somerville, and Botany. Since 2020, it has been held by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who easily won re-election with a margin of 24,769 votes. National also won a majority of the party vote at 58%, more than double second-placed Labour’s 22%. The electorate is diverse, boasting a higher proportional Pasifika and Asian population than the rest of New Zealand.
description_fact_check: "margin of 24,769" (that figure is the winner’s vote total) — the official 2023 majority was 16,337 votes over Kharag Singh.

electorates.name: Christchurch Central
electorates.description: Christchurch Central covers much of inner Christchurch as well as bits from adjoining suburbs such as Sydenham, Beckenham, and Richmond. The electorate has been held by Labour’s Duncan Webb since 2017, who won re-election with 15,553 votes in 2023. National won the party vote in 2023 with 31%, followed by Labour at 28%. In 2011, preliminary results saw a tie on election night, with special votes eventually giving the electorate to National for the first time in its history by just 2 votes.

electorates.name: Christchurch East
electorates.description: Christchurch East covers many of Christchurch's eastern suburbs, including Avondale, New Brighton, and Waimari Beach. The electorate has been held by Labour’s Reuben Davidson, who was first elected in 2023 with a margin of 13,418 votes. Labour also won the party vote in 2023 with 34%, followed by National on 29%. The last party other than Labour to win the seat was the now-defunct Liberal party in 1922.
description_fact_check: "margin of 13,418" — the official 2023 majority was 2,397 votes over Matt Stock.

electorates.name: Coromandel
electorates.description: Coromandel covers the Coromandel peninsula, the Hauraki district, and some of the Bay of Plenty, finishing at the edge of Tauranga. Its main population centres include towns such as Thames, Waihi, and Katikati. National’s Scott Simpson has held the electorate since 2011, being re-elected in 2023 with a margin of 24,914 votes. National also won the party vote in 2023 with 43% of the vote, followed by Labour on 20%. The seat has only ever been held by National in the modern era, barring a three year stint where former Green Party leader Jeanette Fitzsimon eked out a 200-vote victory (Labour did not campaign for the electorate vote that year).

electorates.name: Dunedin
electorates.description: Dunedin covers all but the southern most suburbs of Dunedin city. The electorate is held by Labour’s Rachel Brooking, initially a list MP who was elected in 2023 with a margin of 17,111 votes. Labour also won the party vote with 31%, followed by the Greens on 27%. The electorate skews heavily left; in the two elections with this iteration of the electorate, National has only ever come third to Labour and the Greens in the party vote.

electorates.name: East Cape
electorates.description: East Cape covers the central North Island’s east coast centres, including towns such as Whakātane, Ōpotiki, and Gisborne. The electorate has been established for this election, however its predecessor East Coast electorate was won by National’s Dana Kirkpatrick by a margin of 17,007 votes. Kirkpatrick will stand for East Cape in 2026. The electorate previously existed between 1978 and 1990.

electorates.name: East Coast Bays
electorates.description: East Coast Bays covers the north east areas of Auckland city, covering suburbs such as Albany, Pinehill, and Lucas Creek. It has been held by National’s Erica Stanford since 2017, who won re-election in 2023 with a margin of 27,687 votes. National won a majority of the party vote in 2023 with 58%, while Labour was a distant second at 14%. The electorate was one of the few electorates to be won by a third party in the pre-MPP era, with Social Credit holding the seat between 1980 and 1984.

electorates.name: Epsom
electorates.description: Epsom covers central and eastern Auckland, including the suburbs of Remuera, Mount Eden, and Grafton. Act party leader David Seymour has held the seat since 2014, being re-elected in 2023 with a margin of 17,826 votes. National won the party vote in 2023 with 52%, followed by Labour on 15%. Since the seat was created in 1996, it has returned at least one list MP in every election.
description_fact_check: "margin of 17,826" (that figure is the winner’s vote total) — the official 2023 majority was 8,142 votes over Paul Goldsmith.

electorates.name: Glendene
electorates.description: Glendene covers west Auckland suburbs, including Avondale, Kelston, and the Te Atatū peninsula. The electorate was founded for the first time in 2026, though its predecessor electorates of Te Atatū and Kelston were only ever held by Labour in the MMP era. In 2023, the now disestablished seat of Kelston was won by Labour's Carmel Sepuloni, who is running in the Glendene seat in 2026.

electorates.name: Hamilton East
electorates.description: Hamilton East covers Hamilton’s urban eastern half, up to the Waikato River and covers suburbs such as Claudelands, Flagstaff, and Enderly. National’s Ryan Hamilton is the current MP and was first elected in 2023 with a margin of 17,950. National won the party vote in 2023 with 43% of the vote, followed by Labour with 25%. RyanHamilton is the first MP in New Zealand history to have the same last name as his electorate.

electorates.description: Hamilton West covers Hamilton’s western half, up until the Waikato River which dives it from Hamilton East. It covers suburbs such as Nawtown, Fitzroy, and Melville. Tama Potaka has been the MP since winning the seat in a 2022 by-election and won re-election with a margin of 17,595. National also won the party vote in 2023 with 41% of the vote, followed by Labour on 26%. The seat is regarded as a bellwether seat, as with the exception of 1993, the seat has always been won by the party which won the plurality of the vote.

electorates.name: Henderson
electorates.description: Henderson covers Auckland’s western suburbs, including the areas of Rānui, Lincoln, and Swanson. The electorate has been re-formed for the 2026 election, having not existed since 1993. However, both the historical Henderson electorate and its predecessor Te Atatū and Kelston electorates were almost always held by Labour.

electorates.name: Hutt South
electorates.description: Hutt South covers much of the Lower Hutt region of Wellington, including the suburbs of Gracefield, Waterloo, Eastbourne, and Newlands. It is currently held by National’s Chris Bishop, who won election in 2023 with a margin of 14,772 votes, and who was also the electorate MP from 2017-2020, and being a list MP from 2014. In 2023, the party vote was close, with National winning 34% followed by Labour with 32%. Bishop is only the third-ever MP for Hutt South; his 2017 predecessor Trevor Mallard held it for 21 years before him.

It is one of Aotearoa's longest lasting electorates, having existed continuously in some form since 1866.

electorates.name: Kaipara ki Mahurangi
electorates.description: Kaipara ki Mahurangi covers the satellite towns in the northern Auckland region up to the border to Northland, including Helensville, Warkworth, and Huapai. The electorate is held by National’s Chris Penk, who has held it since the election's creation in 2020 and won in 2023 with a margin of 28,281, but is retiring this election. electorates.name: Kapiti
electorates.description: Kapiti covers the northernmost suburbs of Porirua and the Kapiti Coast, including Paraparaumu, Ōtaki, and Plimmerton. The electorate has been recreated for the 2026 election, and is expected to be competitive as the two predecessor electorates, Mana, and Ōtaki, were safe seats for Labour and National. The predecessor Kapiti electorate, which existed between 1972 and and 1993 was similarly competitive, being held by two MPs for Labour and two MPs for National.

It is held by Labour’s Helen White, initially a list MP who won the electorate vote in 2023 with an 18-vote victory over National’s Melissa Lee, and a total margin of 13,238. National won the party vote with 32%, followed by Labour on 26%, and the Greens on 25%. The electorate has a reputation for producing Labour leaders—Helen Clark, David Shearer, and Jacinda Ardern all held the seat.

The electorate’s very first MP, Henry Powning Stark, holds the record for the shortest time in parliament: he was elected on 19 February 1861 and resigned on 27 April 1861, lasting 67 days.

electorates.description: Nelson covers the area around the city of Nelson, splitting the Tasman region with the West Coast electorate. The seat is held by Labour’s Rachel Boyack, who was first elected in 2020 and narrowly won re-election by 26 votes in 2023, with a total of 17,541. National won the party vote with 32%, followed by Labour on 29%. The electorate is the only one which has existed continuously in every election since New Zealand’s first parliamentary election in 1851.

electorates.name: Waikato
electorates.description: Waikato covers much of the area between Tauranga and Hamilton, including communities such as Morrinsville, Matamata, and Huntly. The seat is held by National’s Tim van de Molen, who was first elected in 2017 and was re-elected in 2023 with a margin of 27,335. National won the party vote in 2023 with 50%, followed by Labour on 18%. The seat boasted the odd distinction of being the birthplace of both 2020 Labour and National leaders Jacinda Ardern and Judith Collins, though neither ran in the electorate.

electorates.name: Waimakariri
electorates.description: Waimakariri covers the area directly north of Christchurch, including towns such as Kaiapoi, Rangiora, as well as a few suburbs of Christchurch such as Northwood and Belfast. The seat is held by National’s Matt Doocey, who was first elected in 2014 and was re-elected in 2023 with a margin of 26,816. National won the party vote in 2023 with 43%, followed by Labour on 24%. Waimakariri is the home-ownership capital of New Zealand, with 54% of residents owning their own home, compared to 41% nationally.

electorates.name: Wairarapa
electorates.description: Wairarapa covers the south-eastern corner of the North Island, stretching from Waipawa and Waipukurau in the North to Masterton, Martinborough, and Lake Ōnonke in the south. The seat is held by National’s Mike Butterick, who was first elected in 2023 with a margin of 20,313. National won the party vote in 2023 with 39%, followed by Labour with 27%. Between 1999 and 2005, Georgina Beyer, New Zealand’s first transgender MP, held the seat.

electorates.name: Waitākere
electorates.description: Waitākere covers Auckland’s western-most suburbs, including Green Bay, Glen Eden, and Titirangi, before stretching into the eponymous Waitākere ranges to the Tasman. The electorate has been reformed for 2026. The seat is held by retiring National MP Paulo Garcia, who is not running again in Waitākere in 2026. Labour won the party vote in Kelston in 2023 with 37%, followed by National on 31%. This is Waitākere’s fourth spell of existence, having previously existed between 1946-66, 1978-87, and 1993-2014.
description_fact_check: Paulo Garcia was the MP for New Lynn (a predecessor seat), not Waitākere.

electorates.name: Waitaki
electorates.description: Forming a triangle between Dunedin, Timaru, and Queenstown, the Waitaki electorate covers settlements such as Ōamaru, Wānaka, and Cromwell. The seat is held by National’s Miles Anderson, who first won election in 2023 with a margin of 22,675. National won the party vote with 43%, followed by Labour with 21%. The electorate uses solar power for heating, more so than any other electorate in the country.
description_fact_check: "margin of 22,675" (that figure is the winner’s vote total) — the official 2023 majority was 12,151 votes over Ethan Reille.

electorates.name: Wellington Bays
electorates.description: Wellington Bays covers the southeastern suburbs of Wellington City such as Newtown, Island Bay, Kilbirnie and across the Miramar Peninsula. The electorate was created out of parts of the former Rongotai and Wellington Central electorates when electorate lines were redrawn in 2025. In 2026, Green Party MP Julie Anne Genter won the Rongotai seat with a margin of 2,717 votes; the Green Party won 32% of the votes and Labour won 31%.

electorates.name: Wellington North
electorates.description: Wellington North covers the central business district of Wellington City and both its western and northern suburbs such as Northland, Karori, Wilton, Ngaio and Khandallah. The electorate first existed from 1905 to 1946, and was recreated out of parts of the former Wellington Central and Ōhāriu electorates when electorate lines were redrawn in 2025. Green Party MP Tamatha Paul won the former Wellington Central electorate with a margin of 6,066 votes in 2023. She is competing against Labour’s health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall.

electorates.name: West Coast-Tasman
electorates.description:
West Coast-Tasman stretches down almost the entirety of the South Island’s West Coast, starting from the Tasman region at Motueka, going past Westport, Greymouth, and Hokitika, before finishing at Haast. The seat is held by National’s Maureen Pugh, a list MP who became an electorate MP in the 2023 election, but is retiring in 2026. Pugh was elected with a margin of 13,317 in 2023. National won the party vote in 2023 with 33% of the vote, followed by Labour with 24%. Geographically, it is the largest general 
electorate in the country.

electorates.name: Whanganui
electorates.description: Whanganui covers its namesake town and the surrounding smaller towns of Hawera and Stratford while also stretching into the Rupaehu district to include Waiouru and Tongariro National Park. The seat is currently held by National’s Carl Bates, who was first elected in 2023 with a margin of 18,484. National won the party vote in 2023 with 39% of the vote, followed by Labour with 28%. The electorate has the highest proportion of the populace employed in manufacturing jobs in the country.

electorates.name: Whangaparāoa
electorates.description: Whangaparāoa covers Auckland’s northern edges, including the communities of Dairy Flat, Hibiscus Coast, and Ōrewa. The electorate is held by National’s Mark Mitchell, who won re-election in 2023 with a margin of 30,742. National won the party vote in 2023 with 53% of the vote, followed by Labour with 15%. Mitchell beat his Labour contender by 23,376 votes in 2023: the largest winning margin of any electorate in 2023.

electorates.name: Whangārei
electorates.description: Surrounded entirely by the Northland electorate, Whangārei forms an alcove around the city of Whangārei and its harbour, and while also stretching south to Waipū and Langs Beach and north to Whangaruru harbour. The seat is held by National’s Shane Reti, who won the electorate back from Labour in 2023 after previously representing it between 2014 and 2020. He is retiring in 2026, after winning election in 2023 with a margin of 20,843. National won the party vote in 2023 with 38%, while Labour came second with 22%. The electorate has the highest proportion of health care and social assistance workers in the country.

electorates.name: Wigram
electorates.description: Wigram covers the south-western suburbs of Christchurch, covering suburbs such as Wigram, Riccarton, Hornby and Sockburn. The seat is currently held by Labour’s Megan Woods, who was first elected in 2011. Woods won in 2023 with 15,590 votes. National won the party vote with 35%, followed by Labour with 29%. The seat is a traditional left-wing stronghold. First formed in 1969, it has only ever been won by a Labour candidate outside the years from 1996 to 2008 that was held by Alliance and Progressive party leader Jim Anderton.

electorates.description: Hauraki-Waikato is a Māori electorate currently held by Labour's Nanaia Mahuta, who won comfortably with a margin of 9,660. In 2020, Labour won the greatest share of party votes in Hauraki-Waikato – 63% to Te Pāti Māori's 12%. The seat was established in 2008 and was previously called Tainui. Mahuta held Tainui since 2002 and Hauraki-Waikato since 2008.

electorates.name: Ikaroa-Rāwhiti
electorates.description: The Ikaroa-Rāwhiti electorate covers the eastern North Island, including Gisborne, Hawke’s Bay, Waiarapa and  parts of the Hutt Valley in Greater Wellington. The seat is currently held by the Labour Party’s Cushla Tangaere-Manuel, who was the only Labour Party candidate to win a Māori seat in 2023. Tangaere-Manuel won 13,747 votes and 54.79% of the party vote. Since its establishment in 1999, the seat has been a stronghold for the Labour Party. The only time Labour has not controlled the seat was when Labour cabinet minister Meka Whaitiri defected to Te Pāti Māori before being defeated in 2023.

In 2023 the seat was won in 2023 by the late Takutai Tarsh Kemp of Te Pāti Māori, who passed away in 2025. The seat is currently held by Te Pāti Māori’s Oriini Kaipara who beat senior Labour MP Peeni Henare 6,948 to 3,429 in the 2025 by-election. Since its establishment in 2002, Labour and Te Pāti Māori have regularly traded the seat.

electorates.name: Te Tai Hauāuru
electorates.description: Te Tai Hauāuru electorate covers the west coast of the North Island. Beginning in South Waikato, the electorate covers the Taranaki, Manawatū-Whanganui, through to Porirua and neighbouring north Wellington suburbs. The seat is held by current Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer who won in 2023 with 16,288 of the vote and 35.05% party vote. The seat was held between 2002 and 2011 by founder of Te Pāti Māori, Tariana Turia.

Kapa-Kingi won with 10,428 votes and 26% of the party vote and is now running as the leader of Te Tai Tokerau Party, having fallen out with Te Pāti Māori leadership.

The seat had traditionally been a strong seat for the Labour Party, with Rino Tirikatene winning from 2011 through until 2023. Tirikatene has recently joined New Zealand First, whose candidate Tutekawa Wyllie won the seat in 1996 and 1999.

1law4all.name: 1Law4All Party
1law4all.intro:
Registered for the 2014 election, it failed to lodge a candidate list after four of five board members resigned
shortly before nominations closed. It had earlier removed references to Allan Titford from its website after his
conviction for rape and arson. As an unregistered group it distributed pamphlets in 2017 and 2019; the Advertising
Standards Authority ordered it to stop the 2019 material as likely to cause "serious offence". [1]

act.name: ACT New Zealand
act.intro: The campaign was launched at Shed 10, Auckland, on 28 June 2026 under the theme **"Lock Labour Out, Unlock New Zealand's Potential"**. Seymour named three focuses: government waste, cutting business restrictions, and equal rights under the law ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/29-06-2026/aura-edits-and-protests-field-notes-from-the-act-partys-big-flash-rally), [speech on Scoop](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2606/S00205.htm)). Broadcaster Paul Henry is fourth on the list. Headline promises, all sourced in [`act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json) and [policies](./policies/README.md):

advance-nz.name: Advance NZ
advance-nz.intro:
Jami-Lee Ross, MP for Botany, left National in 2018 after accusing leader Simon Bridges of corruption over a
$100,000 donation; he was later himself charged by the Serious Fraud Office over the donation scheme and was acquitted
at a High Court trial that began in July 2022, while three co-defendants were convicted. In July 2020 Advance merged campaigns with Billy Te Kahika's NZ Public
Party, a party known for spreading COVID-19 "plandemic" misinformation; other component parties were the NZ People's
Party, Reset NZ and Direct Democracy NZ. [1][2]

alliance.name: Alliance
alliance.intro:
The Alliance was Jim Anderton's left-wing grouping that won 18% of the vote (but only two seats under first-past-the-post)
in 1993, won about 8% and ten seats in 1999 and entered coalition with Labour, introducing paid parental leave and
Kiwibank. It split in 2002 when Anderton's faction left (the Progressives), and
the rump lost all its seats. [1]

animal-justice.name: Animal Justice Party
animal-justice.intro:
The party's 2023 platform included banning recreational fishing and hunting competitions, rodeo, horse racing, fur and
leather production and animal experimentation; supporting the greyhound-racing ban; ending intensive winter grazing
("mud farming") and factory farming; opposing 1080; a commissioner for animals; and a phased shift from animal farming
to plant-based agriculture with support for farmers. It also campaigns against the coalition government's plan to
reverse the 2023 live-export ban. [1]

balance-new-zealand.name: Balance New Zealand

ban-1080.name: Ban 1080 Party
ban-1080.intro:
The party wanted the Department of Conservation's aerial 1080 programme stopped immediately and replaced with
species-specific protection plans and targeted pest control. Its best candidate result was Pete Salter's 6.5% (fourth)
in West Coast-Tasman in 2014. Police visited party officials in 2015 during the investigation into threats to
contaminate infant formula with 1080; the threats were found to be unrelated to the party. After the 2017 result it
deregistered, and many supporters moved to the [Outdoors Party](../nz-outdoors-freedom/README.md). [1][2]

build-the-nation.name: Build the Nation
build-the-nation.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026 (Wikipedia lists Richard McIntosh under 'Build the Nation'; policy.nz lists him as an independent).

civilian.name: The Civilian Party
civilian.intro:
The party drew criticism in 2014 for receiving $33,635 of broadcasting funding; John Key quipped "the biggest joke's
on us, the taxpayer". Uffindell replied that other "joke parties" were getting funding too. It won 1,096 votes (0.05%)
in 2014 and stood no electorate candidates. [1][2]

conservative.name: Conservative Party
conservative.intro:
Businessman Colin Craig, who had organised a 2009 protest march and polled third (8.7%) in the 2010 Auckland mayoralty,
launched the party on 3 August 2011. It absorbed members of the Kiwi Party (Larry Baldock) and New Citizen Party,
spent NZ$1.88 million in 2011 — the second-highest of any party, mostly Craig's own money — and campaigned on raising
the drinking age to 21, parental notification for abortion, repealing the "anti-smacking" law and opposing asset
sales. It won **2.65%**; Craig came second in Rodney. [1]

democracynz.name: DemocracyNZ
democracynz.intro:
King, Northland MP 2017–2020, joined the 2022 anti-mandate protest and left National. In June 2023 five candidates
quit over the party's culture, and many supporters moved to NZ First. DemocracyNZ ran 13 candidates in 2023 and won
**0.24%** (6,786); King came fourth in Northland (3,812 votes). [1][2]

focus-nz.name: Focus New Zealand (Focus NZ, formerly NZ Rural)
focus-nz.intro:
A Northland-based party that stood in the 2013 Far North and Whangārei local elections and the 2014 general election,
where its 639 party votes were the fewest of the 15 registered parties. [1]

free-palestine.name: Free Palestine
free-palestine.intro:
The party was set up in May 2026 to put Gaza and the Palestinian cause at the centre of the 2026 election. On 7 May the
Electoral Commission allocated it $78,887 of broadcasting funding (amended to $82,011), contingent on registration; it
applied in June and was registered on 5 August 2026, but its proposed logo was declined. [1][2]

freedoms-nz.name: Freedoms NZ
freedoms-nz.intro:
Tamaki forecast 20% of the vote. National, Labour, the Greens and ACT all ruled out working with it (National after
initially telling reporters to "read between the lines"). The High Court rejected its challenge to the Electoral
Commission's decision to give the group a single broadcasting allocation. During the 2023 campaign Freedoms NZ supporters,
notably Vision candidate Karl Mokaraka, disrupted Labour, National and ACT events, including Labour's campaign launch.
It won **0.34%** (9,586). [1]

green.name: Green Party
green.intro: The Greens are New Zealand's third-largest party. They have passed the 5% threshold at every election since leaving the Alliance in 1997. Their weakest result was 5.3% in 2005 and their best was 11.6% in 2023. They have helped form three Labour-led governments. Under MMP they have never joined, or given confidence and supply to, a National-led government. The Greens hold four values: ecological wisdom, social justice, grassroots democracy and non-violence. They also accept Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the country's founding document.

heartland.name: Heartland New Zealand Party (HeartlandNZ)
heartland.intro:
Backed at its founding by Hamilton entrepreneur Harry Mowbray, Heartland ran a five-person list in 2020 and won 914
party votes (0.03%), the fewest of any registered party, though Ball polled 8,462 electorate votes (21%, third) in Port
Waikato. [1][2]

independent-taranaki.name: Independent Taranaki
independent-taranaki.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026 (policy.nz lists the candidate as an independent).

internet-party.name: Internet Party
internet-party.intro:
Kim Dotcom — the Megaupload founder whose Auckland home was raided in January 2012 at the request of US authorities —
announced the Internet Party in January 2014. It signed up members through a phone app and was registered on 13 May
2014. Dotcom gave it NZ$3.5 million, described as the largest personal contribution to a New Zealand party on record.
Former Alliance MP and minister Laila Harré was chosen as leader. [1]

jobseeker-party.name: Jobseeker Party

labour.name: Labour Party
labour.intro: Labour's 1916 objective was "the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange"; the socialist objective was dropped in 1951. The current constitution lists democratic-socialist principles — management of natural resources for all, equal access regardless of wealth, co-operation in economic relations "to ensure a just distribution of wealth", the right to work, people "more important than property", **honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi**, international co-operation, and equality regardless of race, sex, sexuality, gender identity, age, religion or disability. Observers describe its policy as pragmatic social democracy with social-liberal positions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

legalise-cannabis.name: Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis
legalise-cannabis.intro:
The ALCP has contested every general election since 1996 and many by-elections without winning a seat. Its best
results were 1.66% (1996) and 1.10% (1999); since then it has stayed below 1%. Former ALCP candidates Nándor Tánczos and
Metiria Turei later became Green MPs (Turei was Green co-leader), and Tim Shadbolt became Invercargill's mayor. Former
deputy leader Abe Gray later joined TOP. [1]

leighton-baker.name: Leighton Baker Party
leighton-baker.intro:
Baker, arrested during the 2022 Wellington protest, launched the party after being replaced as New Conservative
leader. It won **0.07%** (2,105) in 2023; Baker came fourth in Waimakariri (3.9%). He said: "maybe there's not that
many people that agree with us, but we still have an obligation to present a different view." After the election the
Electoral Commission admitted data-entry errors at three booths had wrongly assigned hundreds of votes to the Leighton
Baker Party and New Conservatives (corrected; seat allocation unaffected). See also [Conservative](../conservative/README.md). [1][2][3]

libertarianz.name: Libertarianz
libertarianz.intro:
Libertarianz contested every election from 1996 (best: 0.29% in 1999). In 2006 member Bernard Darnton sued Helen
Clark over Labour's publicly funded 2005 pledge card. Its last general election was 2011 (0.07%). In January 2014 leader
Richard McGrath asked the Electoral Commission to deregister it, saying volunteer administration had become impossible,
and advised members to support ACT under its new president Jamie Whyte. [1]

mana.name: Mana Movement
mana.intro: Party-vote figures: official results as tabulated by Wikipedia (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [4]

money-free-party.name: Money Free Party NZ
money-free-party.intro: Part of the international Money Free movement, which advocates a resource-based economy in which all work is voluntary (inspired by Jacque Fresco's Venus Project). Never registered: it could not verify 500 members for 2014. Results: five electorate candidates in 2014; four in 2017 (293 votes in total); two in 2020 and two in 2023. Osmaston is a frequent mayoral candidate.

nap.name: Not A Party (NAP)
nap.intro: An unregistered 'anti-voting' group (Wikipedia lists its ideology as anti-voting; its website includes posts such as 'Democracy is the worst form of government'). Candidate Richard Goode contested Mana in 2023.

national.name: National Party
national.intro: National is New Zealand's main centre-right party. It is the senior partner in the current coalition government with ACT and NZ First, and it has led a government six times since 1936, more often than any other party. Its 2026 slogan is **"Fixing the Basics. Building the Future."**

new-nation.name: New Nation Party
new-nation.intro:
A founding component of Freedoms NZ, it left in July 2023 to stand on its own and won 1,530 votes (0.05%) — the
lowest of any party in 2023. Its candidate in the 2022 Tauranga by-election, former councillor Andrew Hollis, won 260
votes. [1][2]

new-world-order-mccann-party.name: New World Order McCann Party
new-world-order-mccann-party.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026; Wikipedia links it to the long-running joke 'New World Order Party' label.

newzeal.name: NewZeal
newzeal.intro:
ONE Party launched at Marsden Cross in June 2020, made a reciprocal electorate arrangement with Vision NZ and won
0.28% (8,121). In 2022 it jointly backed a New Conservative candidate in the Hamilton West by-election. Former National
minister **Alfred Ngaro** — who said he was disappointed by National's stance on conversion therapy and gender identity —
took over and renamed it NewZeal in 2023; it won 0.57% (16,126). On 22 March 2026 Ngaro announced at Winston Peters'
State of the Nation speech that he would stand for NZ First, citing "strategic realism and shared values", and the party
deregistered. [1][2]

nz-economic-euthenics-party.name: (NZ) Economic Euthenics
nz-economic-euthenics-party.intro: The label used by perennial Christchurch candidate Tubby Hansen, who contested Wigram in 2023.

nz-independent-coalition.name: NZ Independent Coalition
nz-independent-coalition.intro:
Brendan Horan was expelled from NZ First in December 2012 amid accusations (which he denied) of taking money from his
dying mother's bank account. He formed the party for the 2014 election on the slogan "safe children, safe whanau, safe
society". It won 872 votes (0.04%) and Horan left Parliament. [1][2]

nz-loyal.name: NZ Loyal
nz-loyal.intro:
The party won **1.21%** (34,478 votes) and none of its 33 electorate candidates won. Because it missed the nomination
deadline for most of its intended 15-person list, its official list held only three names (one of whom left the party);
the High Court refused to let it add names after the deadline ("If you leave it to the last minute and something goes
wrong, the responsibility falls squarely on the party"). Had it passed 5%, most of its seats would have been left
empty. [1]

nz-outdoors-freedom.name: NZ Outdoors & Freedom
nz-outdoors-freedom.intro:
The Outdoors Party stood four candidates in 2017 (0.06%). After the Ban 1080 Party deregistered, many of its
supporters joined, and anti-1080 lawyer **Sue Grey** became co-leader around the start of 2020. During 2020 it called the
COVID-19 lockdown "cruel and unreasonable" and compared the government to the Nazi Party; an Auckland rally in June 2020
featured 9/11 "false flag", flat-earth and anti-5G claims and the harassment of a young Asian woman (Grey said those
involved were not party members). Several candidates defected before the 2020 election (0.11%). [1]

nz-peoples-party.name: New Zealand People's Party (2015–2019)
nz-peoples-party.intro:
Nauhria came third (4.2%) in the 2016 Mount Roskill by-election; Winston Peters called the party a "National Party
front". It won 1,890 votes (0.07%) in 2017 with six list candidates and joined Advance NZ in 2020. For the 2026
"People's Party New Zealand" electorate candidates see [peoples-party-new-zealand](../peoples-party-new-zealand/README.md)
— our sources do not establish a connection. [1]

nz-tea-party.name: New Zealand TEA Party (Taxpayers and Entrepreneurs Alliance)
nz-tea-party.intro:
Unconnected to the US Tea Party. Candidate John Palino campaigned for an electorate from Florida. It won 2,414 votes
(0.08%) in 2020. [1][2]

opportunity.name: The Opportunity Party (TOP)
opportunity.intro: Source: official results as tabulated by Wikipedia (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [13]

peoples-party-new-zealand.name: People's Party New Zealand
peoples-party-new-zealand.intro: Two electorate candidates in South Auckland seats. A 'People's Party NZ Inc.' was originally allocated $78,887 of broadcasting money by the Electoral Commission on 7 May 2026, but its amended allocation was $0 because it did not become a registered party. Our sources do not establish whether it is connected to the earlier New Zealand People's Party (2015–19, see ../nz-peoples-party/).

pirate-party.name: Pirate Party of New Zealand
pirate-party.intro:
As an unregistered party it could not contest the party vote. In 2011 it stood in the Botany by-election (32 votes)
and in Hamilton East (137 votes) and Wellington Central (277 votes) at the general election, after being conditionally
awarded $20,000 of broadcasting funding and having its logo registered. It stood no candidates in 2014 and failed to
gain registration for 2017. [1]

progressive-aotearoa-new-zealand.name: Progressive Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (Progressive Aotearoa, PPANZ)
progressive-aotearoa-new-zealand.intro: An unregistered party based on Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar's Progressive Utilization Theory (economic democracy; turning large businesses into co-operatives). It stood two electorate candidates in 2020 (Dyer won 50 votes in Nelson) and Dyer alone in 2023. In August 2026 it announced three candidates. Not to be confused with Jim Anderton's former Progressive Party.

social-credit.name: Social Credit (Democrats for Social Credit / New Zealand Democratic Party for Social Credit)
social-credit.intro:
New Zealand's third party from the 1950s to the 1980s, Social Credit was part of the Alliance from 1991 to 2002 and
briefly of the Progressive Coalition, then re-established itself as an independent party. In this archive's period it
was a fringe party: 0.08% in 2011, 0.07% in 2014, 0.03% in 2017 and 0.05% under the restored Social Credit name in 2020.
In 2021 it opposed COVID-19 vaccine mandates. After deregistration its president Gloria Bruni said it intended to
rebrand to avoid comparison with China's "social credit system". [1][2]

socialist-equality-group.name: Socialist Equality Group

sustainable-nz.name: Sustainable New Zealand Party (Sustainable NZ)
sustainable-nz.intro:
Former party secretary Helen Cartwright alleged in February 2020 that she had been asked to falsify membership records
to reach the 500 needed for registration; Tava said the party complied fully with the Electoral Act. Cartwright left and
founded the Integrity Party. Sustainable NZ received a $53,840 broadcasting allocation and won 1,880 votes (0.07%) in
2020. [1][2]

te-pati-hira.name: Te Pāti Hira

te-pati-maori.name: Te Pāti Māori
te-pati-maori.intro:
Te Pāti Māori is the only party built entirely around Māori political self-determination. Its career has had three
phases:

te-tai-tokerau-party.name: Te Tai Tokerau Party
te-tai-tokerau-party.intro:
Kapa-Kingi won Te Tai Tokerau for [Te Pāti Māori](../te-pati-maori/README.md) in 2023 (by 517 votes over Labour's Kelvin
Davis). After tensions with the party leadership she was suspended in October 2025 and then expelled by its National
Council. policy.nz records that the suspension followed "accusations of mismanaging funds". On 10 March 2026 the High
Court (Justice Paul Radich) ruled the suspension and expulsion unlawful because the process did not follow the party's
kawa and tikanga as its constitution required. Te Pāti Māori accepted the ruling, but in May 2026 Stuff reported that the
two were not working together. [1][2][3]

united-future.name: United Future
united-future.intro:
United Future was formed for the 2002 election by merging Peter Dunne's liberal United New Zealand (founded by
moderate Labour and National MPs in 1995) with Future New Zealand, a "secularised" successor to the Christian
Democrats. Helped by a strong televised-debate performance by Dunne, it won 6.7% and eight seats in 2002, but fell to
2.7% and three seats in 2005 and, after its socially conservative wing (Gordon Copeland, Larry Baldock and others)
left over the 2007 "anti-smacking" law to form what became the Kiwi Party, to a single seat — Dunne's — from 2008.
Dunne then rebranded the party as a moderate centrist party. [1]

vision-nz.name: Vision NZ
vision-nz.intro:
Vision NZ is the third party linked to the Tamakis' Destiny Church, after Destiny New Zealand (2003–07) and the Family
Party (2007–10). Its positions have included opposition to abortion and homosexuality, a call to ban construction of
new mosques, a (later qualified) two-year halt to immigration and refugees, removing non-citizen permanent residents'
right to vote — alongside support for a Māori-owned bank, Tūhoe ownership of Te Urewera and government funding for
Destiny Church programmes. Labour and National ruled out working with it by December 2019. [1]

womens-rights.name: Women's Rights Party
womens-rights.intro:
Jill Ovens, a trade unionist and former Alliance co-leader, resigned from the Labour Party in 2023 over its support for
transgender rights and founded the Women's Rights Party. policy.nz notes that co-leader Dawn Trenberth, also a trade
unionist, had been a Labour member, and that both "left the Labour Party in 2023, feeling alienated by increased
hostility to trans-critical feminist perspectives". [1][2]

your-pic-party.name: Your PIC Party
